name: Blue Glacier (Standard Route)
approach: Start at the Hoh Ranger Station/Hoh Rain Forest trailhead (578 ft) inside Olympic National Park and follow the Hoh River Trail east. The first 10.5 miles, past the Olympus Guard Station (~9.5 mi) to Lewis Meadows (1,005 ft), are gentle, shaded old-growth rainforest walking along the braided, glacially-fed Hoh River, with numerous log/stream crossings and abundant water the whole way. Continue and cross the High Hoh Bridge (a dramatic span hundreds of feet above the gorge, ~13.2 mi) into steeper, more exposed terrain. Reach Elk Lake (2,500 ft) around mile 15, where the trail begins climbing in earnest toward Glacier Meadows (4,200-4,300 ft, ~17.2-17.5 mi), the standard base camp. In early season expect several steep, consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows requiring an ice axe and crampons. About 0.25 mile before Glacier Meadows the trail crosses a washout/slide area via a roughly 100 ft ladder (sometimes called the Jemrod Gully ladder) supplemented by a fixed rope; this is the crux of the hike-in for many parties. From Glacier Meadows, follow the climbers' way trail about 0.8 mile up onto the crest of the lateral moraine (a narrow, exposed 'catwalk' with loose rock underfoot), then along the moraine crest roughly 0.2 mile before descending onto the toe of the Blue Glacier itself (watch for rockfall on this descent). No camping is permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier. From Glacier Meadows the summit is roughly 4-6 more miles and about 3,700 ft of gain, roped up for crevasse travel from the glacier's edge, by way of Snow Dome (~6,600 ft) and the upper mountain; a notable hazard en route is a large crevasse near Crystal Pass that is often 'impassable' except via a snow bridge that must be scouted each season. Late June to mid-August is the best window for a straightforward glacier crossing.
descent: Descend the same North Ridge/Blue Glacier line in reverse. From the base of the ~80 ft summit rock, the roughly Class 4 with one Class 5 (5.4-ish) step is reversed by rappel rather than downclimbed by most parties: build/clip the fixed summit anchor (recent parties note slung horns/blocks and a semi-permanent thin rappel line has appeared in some seasons, though this should not be trusted blindly) and rappel the north side of the summit block. A single-strand rappel with a 40-50m rope reaches the notch/belay ledge for most of the season; a 60m rope (doubled, ~30m per strand) is the safer bet as summer progresses and snow recedes below the block, and some parties join two ropes to make one long rappel to the base of the block instead of two shorter ones. An alternative is a single-rope rappel off the northwest edge to a belay ledge, then downclimbing the original route. Anchor material is a mix of fixed slings on horns/chockstones and natural gear (small cams in the 0.3-0.4 range have been used to back up or build anchors) rather than bolts — inspect any in-place tat before trusting it. Below the summit block, reverse the snow slope (mind the runout) back to the Snow Dome plateau, re-rope for the Blue Glacier crossing, regain the lateral moraine catwalk, and retrace the Hoh River Trail 17+ miles back to the trailhead, watching for the ladder/washout section and any lingering steep snow between Glacier Meadows and Elk Lake.
hazards: glacier crevasse fall
rockfall on summit pyramid
long remote approach
hard glacier ice late season

Crevassed Snow Dome terrain is prone to frequent whiteout, making route-finding a recurring difficulty; some lines off Snow Dome (e.g. Fourth of July, Autobahn) are only viable very early season before bergschrunds open

waysIn.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows
waysIn.season: Jun-Aug
waysIn.notes:
Hoh Rain Forest trailhead (about 578 ft) inside Olympic National Park. The Hoh River Trail runs east; the first ten and a half miles to Lewis Meadows are gentle old-growth walking beside the braided river, with water the whole way. Past the Olympus Guard Station the High Hoh Bridge crosses the gorge and the ground steepens. Elk Lake sits around mile 15 at 2,500 ft, and the trail then climbs in earnest to Glacier Meadows at 4,200-4,300 ft, about mile 17.2-17.5, which is the standard base camp.

About a quarter mile below Glacier Meadows the trail crosses a washout on a ladder of roughly 100 ft with a fixed rope beside it. For many parties that is the hardest part of the walk in.

In early season there are several steep, consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows that want an axe and crampons.

A wilderness permit is required year-round for every overnight stay in Olympic National Park, obtained in advance through Recreation.gov or a Wilderness Information Center, and the Hoh is one of the areas that runs on a daily quota. Camping is not permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier.
hazards: roughly 100 ft ladder plus fixed rope at the washout below Glacier Meadows
steep consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows in early season
narrow, loose lateral moraine crest with rockfall on the descent to the glacier toe
no camping permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier

waysIn.name: Glacier Meadows to the summit block via Snow Dome and Crystal Pass
waysIn.season: Late Jun-mid Aug for straightforward glacier travel
waysIn.notes:
Rope up at the toe of the Blue Glacier and travel up to Snow Dome around 6,600-6,800 ft. This is roped crevasse travel throughout. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is often passable only on a snow bridge, and that bridge has to be scouted afresh each season.

Olympic National Park points climbers at the Crystal Pass line as the standard: from Snow Dome over Crystal Pass, then traversing immediately south of and below Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit, and finally onto the true summit block of the West Peak. It is longer than the alternatives and generally regarded as the safer option through most of the season.
hazards: crevasses throughout - a large crevasse near Crystal Pass often crossable only on a snow bridge that must be scouted each season
bergschrund or moat immediately below the summit block, variable through the season
loose deteriorating scree on the block and on the pinnacle east of it - rockfall onto your own party
the true summit is hidden from the north, so navigation is to a point you cannot see
the false summit is east of the true summit and catches parties out

name: Mount Pilchuck Trail (Standard Route)
approach: From Granite Falls, follow WA-92 east and then the Mountain Loop Highway roughly 10-11 miles to the Verlot Public Service Center. Continue about 1 mile past Verlot, cross the South Fork Stillaguamish River, and turn right (south) onto Mount Pilchuck Road (FR 42). Follow FR 42 for about 6.8 miles — rough, washboarded gravel for the first ~4.7 miles and paved for the last ~1.9, with the gravel's condition varying by year — to the Mount Pilchuck Trailhead parking area (roughly 3,000-3,100 ft). In years when FR 42 is gated below the trailhead (common in shoulder season), the hike instead starts from the Heather Lake Trailhead, adding roughly 5 miles and substantial elevation gain each way.
descent: From the lookout, reverse the short ladder and boulder-field scramble, then follow the marked trail (orange blazes across the open boulder field, then single-track through forest) back down to the trailhead parking area. Do not attempt to shortcut down the old ski-area clearing visible west of the trail — it looks like a shortcut but is steep and brushy, and has contributed to lost-hiker rescues.
hazards: Fatal falls have occurred on the exposed final scramble/lookout rocks, including in wet or icy conditions (e.g. a 2015 fall of roughly 400 ft near the lookout).
Snohomish County Volunteer Search and Rescue is called to Mount Pilchuck multiple times per season, mostly for lost or injured hikers on the boulder field and old ski-slope area.
Snow can obscure the trail and boulder-field route markers into early summer, leading to route-finding errors.

waysIn.name: Mount Pilchuck Road to the trailhead
waysIn.season: July to October. The trail is typically snow-covered into early or midsummer in some years, and traction is commonly needed through June.
waysIn.notes: From Granite Falls take the highway east and then the Mountain Loop about ten or eleven miles to the ranger station. Continue about a mile past it, cross the river, and turn south onto the Mount Pilchuck road. Follow it roughly seven miles — a mix of paved and rough washboarded gravel that varies year to year with maintenance — to the trailhead parking area at around three thousand feet.
hazards: Fatal falls have occurred on the exposed final scramble and lookout rocks, particularly in wet or icy conditions
Search and rescue is called to this peak several times a season, mostly for lost or injured parties on the boulder field and the old ski-slope ground
Snow obscures the trail and the painted boulder-field markers into early summer
The fixed ladder's rungs can spin underfoot

waysIn.name: From the Heather Lake trailhead when the road is gated
waysIn.season: Shoulder season, when the forest road is closed below the trailhead — common in spring and autumn.
waysIn.notes: In years when the road is gated below the trailhead, the walk starts from the Heather Lake trailhead instead, adding roughly five miles and substantial gain each way. Everything above the normal trailhead is identical, so this is a road-walk variant rather than a different climb, but it changes a half-day into a long one and is worth confirming before driving out.
hazards: A much longer day than the standard start, with the same exposed finish at the end of it
Same fall and route-finding hazards on the boulder field and summit rocks
Snow more likely on the upper mountain in the shoulder seasons when this variant applies
waysIn.whyThisWay: In winter and shoulder seasons when the forest road is closed to vehicles below the normal trailhead, forcing a long extra walk up the road.

name: South Ridge / Southeast Ridge
approach: From Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20, MP 134) hike the Ross Lake shoreline trail ~7 mi to the Big Beaver Trail junction (or take the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver Landing to shorten this), then continue ~5 mi up Big Beaver Trail to Thirtynine Mile Creek/Camp. Leave the trail there and climb a brushy forested rib to gain the south ridge at a ~6,600 ft saddle. Round trip from the Big Beaver Landing water-taxi drop is roughly 18 miles with 7,000+ ft of elevation gain, typically done over 2-3 days; walking the lakeshore both ways instead adds about 14 miles. From the saddle, follow the ridge crest (Class 1-2) past points 7,361 ft and 7,547 ft to a short Class 3 step below the true summit; Luna Camp, about 5 miles farther up Big Beaver Trail, is the start of the separate Southwest Rib route, not this one.
descent: Reverse the ascent: follow the ridge crest back down past the two intermediate high points, with the short Class 3 step below the summit taken carefully on the way down, to the saddle around 6,600 ft. Drop the brushy forested rib to Thirtynine Mile Creek, the last reliable water, and rejoin Big Beaver Trail. From there it is about 5 miles of trail back toward Ross Lake, and the lakeshore trail or the water taxi from Big Beaver Landing completes the exit. Loose rock on the upper ridge is a rockfall hazard for anyone below you, and the brush on the rib is slow in the dark.
hazards: routefinding through forest and along the ridge crest
afternoon thunderstorms
cornices on the south ridge in early/mid season (largely melted out by July)

waysIn.name: Big Beaver valley to Thirtynine Mile Creek, then the ridge
waysIn.season: Mid-July through September, once the cornices on the south ridge have melted out and the talus in the upper cirque is clear.
waysIn.notes: From the Ross Dam Trailhead the trail drops to the lake and follows the shoreline to the Big Beaver Trail junction; a water taxi to the Big Beaver landing removes that shoreline stretch and is what most parties use. The Big Beaver Trail then runs up the valley through old growth to Thirtynine Mile Creek and its camp, which has tent sites on the west bank and a stock camp on the east, and is the last reliable running water and the last legal campsite before you leave the trail. Leave the tread between the creek crossing and the camp marker post and climb north through a brushy gully and the rib beside it — this low section is a genuinely horrible bushwhack and it is where the bulk of the day's gain happens. Travel eases considerably once you break out on the ridge crest above, where open forest and then open walking carry you over the intermediate points to the saddle where the rib meets the south ridge proper. An informal saddle campsite there splits the climb into two days, but it has no running water, so carry up from the creek.
hazards: route-finding through forest and along the ridge crest, with no marked line anywhere above the trail
cornices on the south ridge in early and mid season
afternoon thunderstorms on an open crest
a brushy, steep departure from the valley trail that is easy to lose in either direction
no water above Thirtynine Mile Creek

name: South Side
approach: Two camps are used: Silver Lake (6,763 ft, reached via a long Silver Creek bushwhack from Ross Lake) or Ouzel Lake (5,700 ft, reached via the Depot Creek approach from Chilliwack Lake Road, BC — the easier of the two to reach). From Ouzel Lake, climb northeast up an obvious wide gully to the 7,380-ft Custer-Spickard saddle, then traverse and ascend southwestward below the Custer-Rahm ridge to the roughly 7,400-ft upper terrace. From Silver Lake, climb above the lakeside cliffs to the northwest, or walk the north shore west until the cliffs end, then climb talus/slabs north to the same terrace.
descent: No rappel anchors are reported in the crux gully; downclimb it (the alternate, longer Class 3 gully just downhill and right of it may be an easier downclimb than the Class 4/5 line). From the upper terrace, reverse the traverse back down to the Custer-Spickard saddle and Ouzel Lake camp, or to Silver Lake, or continue over to Mount Custer if adding it to the day.
hazards: Rockfall and loose rock in the Class 4/5 crux gully, especially when wet
Steep snowfield in the upper basin can be icy in early season

waysIn.name: Depot Creek from the Canadian side
waysIn.notes: The unmaintained Depot Creek trail crosses the border to Ouzel Lake, then the bench leads east to the south side. The easiest and most used way, but it means crossing the border on foot away from a port of entry, so confirm the entry rules first, and the road needs high clearance.
hazards: Rockfall and loose rock in the Class 4/5 crux gully, especially when wet
No rappel anchors reported in the crux gully; it must be downclimbed
Steep snowfield in the upper basin can be icy early season
Border crossing on foot away from a port of entry; high-clearance road to the trailhead
Ouzel Lake camp reached by an unmaintained trail; Custer-Spickard saddle and terrace traverse are cross-country
waysIn.whyThisWay: Usually the shortest way, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

waysIn.name: Silver Creek from Ross Lake
waysIn.notes: The all-US way: a water taxi up Ross Lake to the mouth of Silver Creek, then a long bushwhack up Silver Creek to Silver Lake and north to the upper terrace. Harder and much brushier.
hazards: Long, brushy bushwhack up Silver Creek to Silver Lake; harder than the other way in
Water taxi up Ross Lake needed to reach the mouth of Silver Creek
Climbing above lakeside cliffs or talus and slabs to reach the upper terrace
Rockfall and loose rock in the Class 4/5 crux gully, especially when wet
No rappel anchors reported in the crux gully; steep snowfield in the upper basin can be icy early season

name: Curtis Ridge
approach: From White River Campground (reached via WA-410 and White River Road — check the park's current road status for early/late-season openings), hike the Glacier Basin Trail roughly 3.5 miles and about 1,700 ft of gain to Glacier Basin (~5,900 ft), a broad basin with the last reliable running water and a common camping spot. From there, continue on climbers' path up to St. Elmo Pass (~7,400 ft), gaining another ~1,500 ft over roughly a mile of steepening scree/snow. At St. Elmo Pass, rope up for glacier travel: drop down onto the Winthrop Glacier and contour west/southwest, threading around crevasses, to reach the base of Curtis Ridge on its east (Winthrop) side. This is the same approach corridor used for Liberty Ridge, so expect other parties and established boot tracks in season. Above St. Elmo Pass there is no water; carry enough for the climb or plan to melt snow.
descent: Curtis Ridge tops out onto the upper mountain near the Winthrop/Emmons basin, and the standard descent is to continue over the summit area and down the Emmons-Winthrop Glacier route to Camp Schurman, then follow the established boot path down the Inter Glacier back toward Glacier Basin and out to White River. This is a walk-off/glissade descent, not a rappel descent — many parties glissade a substantial chunk (roughly 2,000-3,000 vertical feet) of the Inter Glacier snowfield above Glacier Basin when conditions allow, which is the fastest way off the mountain on this side. No fixed rappels are used; standard crevasse-rescue gear covers the glacier sections.
hazards: Long, committing ridge with serac-threatened sections below the Willis Wall icecap
Loose rock and mixed ground
Complex route-finding and remote position
Rockfall is concentrated immediately after descending onto the Winthrop Glacier, partway through, and at the end of the traverse — move quickly through these zones
Longitudinal crevasses and gaping moats on the Winthrop Glacier traverse

waysIn.name: White River, Glacier Basin, St Elmo Pass and the Winthrop Glacier traverse
waysIn.season: Roughly May-Jun, in cold stable conditions when the rock is frozen in place
waysIn.notes:
From White River Campground, hike the Glacier Basin Trail about 3.5 miles and 1,700 ft to Glacier Basin near 5,900 ft — a broad basin with the last reliable running water and a common camp. Continue on climbers' path up to St Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, another 1,500 ft over roughly a mile of steepening scree and snow.

At the pass, rope up. Drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and contour west and southwest between roughly 7,200 and 7,400 ft, threading crevasses, to reach the base of Curtis Ridge on its east side.

This is the same corridor Liberty Ridge parties use, so in season there is often a boot track and other parties on it. Above St Elmo Pass there is no water at all.

Rockfall on the traverse concentrates in three places: immediately after you drop onto the glacier, roughly halfway across, and at the far end. Move through those, do not rest in them.
hazards: Serac-threatened sections below the Willis Wall icecap
Loose rock and mixed ground with complex route-finding
Rockfall concentrated at three points on the Winthrop traverse
Longitudinal crevasses and gaping moats running along the line of travel
Remote position with a long exit and no water above St Elmo Pass

name: Emmons–Winthrop Glacier
approach: From White River Campground (4,400 ft) on SR 410, the Glacier Basin Trail climbs 3.5 miles through forest along the Inter Fork of the White River — several creek crossings and old avalanche/slide paths cross the trail — to Glacier Basin Campground (5,935 ft), which has six designated sites, a camp toilet, and a bear-proof food cache; this is the last reliable water source and the last forested camp. From Glacier Basin, a climbers' path continues about a mile up the prominent (often yellowish, when melted out) lateral moraine toward the toe of the Inter Glacier (~7,000 ft), then climbs the glacier itself — roughly 1,500 ft of moderate, generally lower-crevasse-hazard snow slope — to Camp Curtis on the glacier's rim (~8,700 ft). From Camp Curtis the route descends slightly and traverses onto the Emmons Glacier, rounding the south side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Schurman (9,460–9,600 ft), the high camp, marked by an NPS ranger hut and toilet, with tent platforms typically dug into snow on the Emmons side of the rocky prow. Both the Inter Glacier and the Emmons traverse are crevassed and roped travel is standard; the Inter Glacier is the milder of the two but still opens real crevasses as the season progresses.
descent: The Emmons-Winthrop is climbed and descended on the same line — a glacier walk-down, not a technical descent, with no rappelling required on a normal season's route. From the summit, parties descend the broad upper Emmons slope back through 'the Corridor' to Camp Schurman; this upper stretch is the crux of the descent not technically but navigationally, since the glacier is heavily crevassed above roughly 12,000 ft and the exact line shifts through the season, so a current GPS track down is strongly recommended. From Camp Schurman, reverse the approach: up and around the south side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Curtis, down the Inter Glacier, and out via Glacier Basin to White River Campground. NPS incident records repeatedly flag this route's biggest descent hazard as simple wayfinding — the boot path isn't maintained or wanded, and even experienced Emmons-Winthrop parties have needed SOS rescue after losing the route in whiteout on this exact stretch. Below Camp Curtis, the Inter Glacier can often be glissaded in good afternoon snow conditions, cutting real time off the walk-out. No rappels are involved.
hazards: Large open crevasses and weak snow bridges, especially mid-to-late season
The Corridor and upper glacier carry avalanche and collapse hazard after storms
Serac fall near the Winthrop icefall
Long, sustained glacier travel — fatigue-related falls on descent
Bergschrund crossing near 13,000 ft on the upper Emmons, usually snow-bridged; becomes a more distinct obstacle as crevasses open later in the season.

waysIn.name: White River Campground, Glacier Basin, Inter Glacier and Camp Schurman
waysIn.season: Late spring through August, once the White River road and campground are open and before summer melt opens the upper crevasse fields
waysIn.notes:
The Glacier Basin trailhead is in Loop D of White River Campground (about 4,300–4,400 ft), reached by the White River road off SR 410. That road and the campground are seasonal and open on the snowpack, not on a date.

The trail follows the Inter Fork of the White River on an old mining road grade, 3.5 miles to Glacier Basin Campground (~5,935 ft): six designated sites, a toilet and a bear-proof food cache. This is the last reliable water and the last forested camp.

Above Glacier Basin a climbers' path continues about a mile up the lateral moraine — conspicuously yellowish once it melts out — to the toe of the Inter Glacier at roughly 7,000 ft. The Inter Glacier is about 1,500 ft of moderate snow; it is the mildest glacier on the route but it opens real crevasses as the season goes on, and roped travel is standard. It leads to Camp Curtis on the rim at about 8,700 ft.

From Camp Curtis the route drops slightly and traverses onto the lower Emmons Glacier, rounding the southern side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Schurman (about 9,460 ft), where the Emmons and Winthrop glaciers split around the Prow. There is an NPS ranger hut, an emergency radio on the front of it, toilets and a blue-bag barrel; tent platforms are dug into snow on the Emmons side.

Camp Schurman's nightly capacity is small — far smaller than Camp Muir's — so a permit here is worth reserving. The same Rainier permit structure applies: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, plus a wilderness permit for each overnight.
hazards: Crevasses on the Inter Glacier, which open through the season despite its mild reputation
Loose, brittle volcanic rock on the direct scramble down the Prow into Camp Schurman
Rockfall onto the moraine path above Glacier Basin
Crevasse maze above 12,000 ft where the Corridor ends
Bergschrund near 13,000 ft, which can be impassable direct in late season
Creek crossings and old slide paths on the Glacier Basin trail

name: Kautz Glacier
approach: Two approaches are used, both arduous. The Paradise approach (5,420 ft) follows the Skyline Trail to the Nisqually Moraine Trail, then a climbers' path along the moraine to about 6,300 ft, where several boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier itself; most parties rope up here, since the crossing threads through heavily crevassed terrain exposed to icefall from above and is genuinely dangerous in reduced visibility. From the glacier's east moraine there are two ways up onto Wapowety Cleaver: a flat traverse to the base of 'The Fan,' a gully with avalanche, rockfall, and steep-slope hazard, climbed directly to a bench at 7,300 ft; or a climb up the Nisqually/Wilson Glacier margin at 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft 'Wilson Bench.' From the bench, snow slopes lead to the ridge crest and a string of established camps at increasing elevation — Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft), and the Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft, the most common base for a summit push, with running water from mid-June on). The alternative Van Trump Park approach starts at the Comet Falls Trailhead (3,650 ft): follow the maintained Comet Falls Trail 2.2 miles (2,000 ft gain) to a junction, continue toward Van Trump Park another 0.6 miles to where maintained trail ends, then follow unmaintained social trails up a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, followed up to the Upper Castle (9,500 ft) where the two approaches merge — descending this line requires a saved GPS track to relocate the correct moraine and treeline trail junction, even in good visibility, per NPS guidance. Above the Castle, the Turtle Snowfield (slopes up to 45°) is climbed on its west (climber's-left) side, close to the rock ridge, since its center and climber's-right (east) side are threatened by ice and rockfall from above. Established high camps continue at Camp Hazard (10,800 ft, on the climber's-left side at the top of the Turtle Snowfield), the Rock Step camps (11,250 ft), and exposed Wapowety Cleaver bivy sites (13,100 ft, used mainly by parties planning to descend via the Disappointment Cleaver rather than reverse the Kautz).
descent: Descending the Kautz is a real technical descent, not a walk-off, and involves multiple rappels through the ice chute — typically two to five depending on conditions, ice quality, and rope length. From the top of Wapowety Cleaver, parties reverse the glacier line down through crevassed terrain to the top of the ice chute, then find easier ground to climber's-left/east to belay into the chute rather than committing to team-arrest on exposed ice. The upper ice step (commonly a short pitch up to 300+ ft of AI3 alpine ice) is rappelled: the NPS route brief states this takes anywhere from one to three rappels depending on rope length and how many ropes the team carries, using 'Zero-Thread' ice anchors — a variant of the V-thread/Abalakov anchor chosen because it's equally strong but leaves no gear behind; there is no fixed/bolted hardware on this route, and the Park Service explicitly discourages leaving V-thread anchors in place between ascent and descent since they can melt out. Below the upper step, lower-angle snow leads to the lower ice step, typically descended with one to two more rappels on the same anchor style — so two to five rappels total through the chute is realistic for most parties on a single 60m rope, fewer with two ropes or more if short-pitching. After the chute, a fast, alert traverse back toward the Rock Step is required, since this stretch sits directly under the active Kautz Ice Cliff. Climbing back up through the Rock Step itself (awkward 5th-class moves protected by fixed rope and old slings on rock anchors) returns parties to high camp; from there it's a walk/glissade down the Turtle Snowfield, back across the Nisqually or Wilson glacier crossing, and out to Paradise (or back down through Van Trump Park). A significant number of teams instead choose the 'up-and-over' option — descending the easier, non-technical Disappointment Cleaver/Muir Snowfield line from the summit to Camp Muir and Paradise — specifically to avoid re-descending the ice chute and Rock Step on tired legs, at the cost of having to haul full camping gear over the summit.
hazards: The Kautz ice chute — firm alpine ice, in two steps, each anywhere from a short pitch to a few hundred feet depending on the year, and bare and hard late season
Rock and icefall off the Kautz Ice Cliff and Wapowety Cleaver, worst once the sun hits
Crevasse navigation on the upper Nisqually and Kautz glaciers
Year-to-year variability: in lean years the ice steepens and lengthens
Moat/bergschrund at the base of the Kautz Ice Chute where it meets the glacier below — check current condition before committing.

waysIn.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson bench
waysIn.season: Mid-May into early August; the approach and glaciers deteriorate quickly after that
waysIn.notes:
From Paradise (5,420 ft) follow the paved trail about a mile to Glacier Vista, then the Nisqually Moraine climbers' path to roughly 6,300 ft where boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier. Rope up here — the crossing is through crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above and is dangerous in poor visibility.

From the east side of the glacier there are two ways onto the Wapowety Cleaver ground. One is a flat traverse to the base of a gully known as The Fan, climbed directly to a bench at about 7,300 ft; The Fan carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard. The other climbs the Nisqually/Wilson margin at about 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft bench.

Above the bench, snow slopes lead to a string of established camps: Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft) and Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft), the most common base, with running water from about mid-June. Higher again, rock islands along the west edge of the Turtle snowfield between roughly 9,500 and 10,500 ft hold good bivouacs, and there is usually flowing water at the snowfield edges in warm weather.

Camp Hazard (about 10,800 ft) is the traditional high camp and is named for what sits above it: the Kautz Ice Cliff. Many parties deliberately camp lower and climb through Camp Hazard early rather than sleep under the cliff. On the Turtle, keep to the western, climber's-left side — the centre and east are raked by ice and rock off the cliff.

Rainier permits apply: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, and a wilderness permit for each overnight camp in the high-use season.
hazards: Nisqually Glacier crossing through heavily crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above, dangerous in poor visibility
The Fan gully carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard
Serac fall from the Kautz Ice Cliff onto Camp Hazard and the traverse beneath it; centre and east of the Turtle are raked by ice and rock
Firm alpine ice in two steps in the Kautz chute, bare and hard late season; thin or rotten ice late
Crevasse navigation on the upper Nisqually and Kautz glaciers; bergschrund at the chute base
Descent by multiple rappels through the ice chute, typically two to five

waysIn.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park
waysIn.season: Same window; avoids the Nisqually Glacier crossing entirely
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Comet Falls trailhead (3,650 ft) on the Longmire–Paradise road. The maintained Comet Falls Trail climbs 2.2 miles and about 2,000 ft to a junction, then continues toward Van Trump Park for another 0.6 miles to the end of maintained tread. From there unmaintained social trails climb a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, which is followed to the Upper Castle at roughly 9,500 ft where this approach merges with the Paradise line.

The advantage is that it never crosses the Nisqually Glacier. The cost is a lower start, a steeper carry and a descent that is genuinely hard to reverse: the Park Service's own advice is to save a GPS track, because relocating the correct moraine and the treeline trail junction on the way down is difficult even in clear weather. Several parties a season lose that junction and end up bushwhacking.
hazards: Steep unmaintained moraine travel above the end of maintained trail near Van Trump Park
Losing the moraine crest and the treeline trail junction on descent; save a track
Starts about 1,700 ft lower, so a steeper carry; avoids the Nisqually crossing
Serac and ice-cliff exposure above the Castle and at Camp Hazard; keep to climber's left on the Turtle
Firm alpine ice in two steps in the Kautz chute, bare and hard late season; bergschrund at the chute base
Crevasses on the Van Trump remnant and upper glaciers; descent by multiple rappels through the chute
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late in the season, when the Nisqually Glacier is broken and rockfall-prone; this starts lower and runs longer but never crosses it, and the trail stays free of snow far up.

name: Liberty Ridge
approach: Start at White River Campground (4,400 ft) off WA-410 (the driving approach is covered separately). Follow the Glacier Basin Trail up the White River valley about 3.5 miles, gaining roughly 1,500 ft, crossing the West Fork White River on a footbridge, to Glacier Basin camp (~5,900 ft) beneath the Inter Glacier — this is the last dependable running water before the route goes onto snow and ice for good. From Glacier Basin the maintained trail ends; leave it and climb snow/scree slopes east toward St. Elmo Pass (~7,400 ft), a boot-track/climber's route (not signed or maintained) between Mt. Ruth and the Inter Glacier that can be icy in early season and can develop cornices. From St. Elmo Pass, drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and contour counter-clockwise (roped glacier travel with crevasse-rescue gear required from here on) beneath Mt. Ruth, crossing the Winthrop and traversing under/around Curtis Ridge to a ramp that accesses the Carbon Glacier at about 7,300 ft — there are established bivy sites in this access gully. This traverse sits below Willis Wall and Ptarmigan Ridge, so icefall and rockfall (worsening as the day warms) are real hazards; parties typically move through early. From the Carbon Glacier access, ascend the glacier as directly as crevasses allow to the base of Liberty Ridge, climb a snow ramp onto the ridge crest from its east side, cross to the west side, and continue up snow slopes and rock outcrops to Thumb Rock (10,775 ft), the standard high camp — flat, wind-sheltered tent sites but no liquid water (melt snow/ice). White River to Thumb Rock is commonly a long single push (7-10+ hours) or split with the Curtis Ridge bivy; expect sustained roped glacier travel, crevasse hazard on the Winthrop and Carbon crossings, and rockfall/icefall exposure under Willis Wall. Above Thumb Rock the ridge steepens through sustained ice runnels past the Black Pyramid rock band before the final steep ice leads onto the upper mountain near Liberty Cap; rockfall/serac hazard grows as the day warms, so climb this section early. In late May the established tracks dropped low on the Winthrop Glacier below its icefall, which avoided the big crevasses on the way to the lower Curtis Ridge.
descent: Liberty Ridge is never descended — its loose rock, sustained steep ice, and total lack of rappel anchors or safe bivy terrain below Thumb Rock make down-climbing the ridge far more dangerous than continuing up and over the mountain; the route's accident history is dominated by a dangerous pattern: parties judge that continuing up feels safer than retreating. From the summit area, the standard descent drops off Liberty Cap's east side about 600 ft to Liberty Saddle, joins the Emmons-Winthrop route, and descends the broad Emmons Glacier via 'the Corridor' to Camp Schurman — an average party needs just under three hours for this leg. From Camp Schurman, parties reverse the Emmons approach: around the south side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Curtis, down the Inter Glacier, and out via Glacier Basin to White River Campground (roughly another 3+ hours). This is a glacier walk-down with no rappelling required in a typical season — the real hazards are crevasse navigation (the Emmons/Winthrop shift through the summer and aren't wanded; a current GPS track is considered essential, and multiple Liberty Ridge parties have needed SOS rescue after losing the route here in whiteout) and large cornices that form on the east side of Liberty Saddle. A minority of parties instead descend the Winthrop Glacier from Camp Schurman toward lower Curtis Ridge/Moraine Park if they've pre-arranged a shuttle, to avoid re-crossing the Inter Glacier, but the Emmons-to-White River line is standard. No rappels on the descent.
hazards: Constant rock and icefall — Liberty Ridge is statistically one of the deadliest routes on the mountain
Serac threat from the Willis Wall and the summit ice cap above the Black Pyramid
Steep firm ice/névé to 60–70° on the upper ridge and the bergschrund
Avalanche on the Carbon Glacier approach and ridge after storms
Committing position — escape becomes very difficult once high on the ridge

waysIn.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and the Carbon Glacier
waysIn.season: Early May to mid-June
waysIn.notes: Everyone walks in from White River Campground, and the walking is over quickly. The Glacier Basin Trail is maintained for about three and a half miles to the basin at roughly 5,900 ft, which holds the last running water you will see until the descent brings you down to Camp Schurman. Above the basin there is no trail: a boot track climbs snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, and from the far side of the pass you drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and stay roped for the rest of the trip. The counter-clockwise traverse under Mount Ruth and around the toe of Curtis Ridge is the part that decides the day, because it runs directly beneath Willis Wall and both walls shed rock and ice more freely once the sun is on them. Most parties split the approach with a bivy on lower Curtis Ridge somewhere between about 7,200 and 7,600 ft, right beside the ramp that drops onto the Carbon Glacier, and it is the only place on the whole approach where you get a head-on look at the route to pick your line. Curtis Ridge is broad and deceptive in cloud and parties repeatedly think they have arrived when they have not; the rule everyone repeats is to stay low and, when in doubt, angle down and right. If what you are looking over is not a mellow fifty-foot talus slope, you are too high, and climbing further only cliffs you out. A climbing permit is required and this line carries its own briefing, so sort both before driving up rather than on the morning you want to leave.
hazards: Rockfall and icefall off Willis Wall onto the Carbon Glacier traverse, worsening as the day warms
Serac collapse off the Liberty Cap Glacier onto the west side of the Carbon basin
Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Winthrop and Carbon crossings; a slip on the Winthrop traverse can mean a long fall
The moat where glacier meets rock at the foot of the ridge can turn parties around
Rockfall into Thumb Rock camp from the tower opposite
Sustained steep ice to about 60 degrees above the Black Pyramid; summit bergschrund crossing
Altitude, and no retreat down the route once above Thumb Rock

waysIn.name: Carbon River and the Wonderland Trail to Curtis Ridge
waysIn.notes: The older way in, used mainly early in the season when the White River road is still closed. From the Carbon River entrance, walk or bike the old road to Ipsut Creek, then follow the Wonderland Trail up the Carbon River to the snout of the Carbon Glacier and onto the ice toward Curtis Ridge. It starts lower and is noticeably longer than the White River approach, and the Carbon River crossing on the Wonderland Trail can be a problem.
hazards: Long approach from the Carbon River entrance: old road, then the Wonderland Trail up the Carbon River
Carbon River crossing on the Wonderland Trail can be a problem
Travel up the Carbon Glacier snout toward Curtis Ridge: crevasses and thin snow bridges
Rockfall and icefall off Willis Wall; do not camp on the open Carbon under the wall
Serac collapse off the Liberty Cap Glacier; the moat at the foot of the ridge
Sustained steep ice to about 60 degrees above the Black Pyramid; summit bergschrund crossing
Altitude, and no retreat down the route once above Thumb Rock
waysIn.whyThisWay: Early in the season while the White River road is still closed; it starts lower and is longer, and the Carbon River crossing on the Wonderland Trail can be a problem.

name: Nisqually Icefall
approach: From Paradise (5,400 ft), follow the Skyline Trail up past Glacier Vista/Pan Point and drop onto the Nisqually Glacier — the standard access point used for both the Nisqually Icefall and the neighboring Wapowety Cleaver routes. Rope up for glacier travel here; there is no maintained trail once you're on ice. Ascend the glacier alongside the Wapowety Cleaver, gaining elevation steadily to around 9,900 ft, where the lower bergschrund marks the start of technical climbing — typically 40-50 ft of steep ice/snow to gain the upper Nisqually icefall. From there the route continues through broken, crevassed terrain in the upper Nisqually basin up toward the top of the Wapowety Cleaver near 13,000 ft. The upper Nisqually basin is the most time-consuming and dangerous section of the whole route: it sits directly under active icefall and rockfall zones, so parties are advised to move through it as quickly as possible rather than stopping to regroup. There's no reliable water source once you leave Paradise; melt snow above the glacier's edge.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel descent. Two options are used: descend the Gibraltar Chute directly back toward Paradise — a direct, mostly non-technical line, though much of the chute is exposed to rock- and icefall so it's not necessarily the 'easy' option it sounds like — or carry over and descend the Disappointment Cleaver route (also to Paradise, same trailhead so no shuttle needed). In late-season, low-snow conditions, guides note a carryover to the DC is often the safer call since travel back down through the icefall itself gets harder and more hazardous as the summer progresses. No rappels are used on either descent option; standard glacier gear (pickets, screws) covers it.
hazards: Active icefall with collapsing seracs
Complex crevasse and serac navigation, including dicey crossings on the upper Nisqually Glacier
Hazard increases rapidly with warming through the day
Documented history of large slide activity in the icefall; considered one of the more circuitous and dangerous lines on the mountain and is rarely climbed in any given season

waysIn.name: Paradise, the Skyline Trail and the Nisqually Glacier to the lower bergschrund
waysIn.season: Roughly May-Jun. This is an early-season line: the icefall wants to be frozen, and hazard rises steeply through the summer as the glacier warms
waysIn.notes:
From Paradise at about 5,400 ft, follow the Skyline Trail up past Glacier Vista and Pan Point, then leave it and drop west onto the Nisqually Glacier. This is the same access point the Wapowety Cleaver lines use. Rope up before you step onto ice; there is no maintained trail from here on and no reliable water once you leave Paradise, so plan on melting snow.

Ascend the Nisqually alongside the Wapowety Cleaver, gaining steadily to about 9,900 ft where the lower bergschrund marks the start of the technical ground — typically 40 to 50 ft of steep ice or snow to gain the icefall itself.

Above that the route threads broken, crevassed terrain in the upper Nisqually basin toward the top of the Wapowety Cleaver near 13,000 ft. That basin is the most time-consuming and the most dangerous section of the whole climb: it sits directly under active icefall and rockfall, and the correct tactic is to move through it without stopping to regroup. The seracs rearrange themselves every season, so expect to find your own way rather than follow anyone's line.
hazards: Active icefall with collapsing seracs directly above the upper basin
Complex crevasse and serac navigation that changes every season
Hazard rises rapidly with warming through the day, so the upper basin must be crossed early
Documented history of large slide activity in the icefall
No reliable water above Paradise

name: Ptarmigan Ridge
approach: The road to Mowich Lake is closed indefinitely: WSDOT permanently closed the Fairfax Bridge on SR 165 on April 22, 2025, and there is no public access to Mowich Lake from SR 165, so the White River side is the only start a car can reach. Historically approached either from the west via Mowich Lake (shorter) or from the east via White River Campground (longer, typically requiring a car shuttle or carryover with descent via the Emmons Glacier). Even before the closure, the summer-only Mowich Lake road usually opened well after this route came into condition, so the White River side, with its much longer walk, was often the practical start anyway.
descent: Ptarmigan Ridge is normally done as a carryover. Once on the summit plateau near the crater rim, descend the Emmons-Winthrop route: down the broad Emmons Glacier, threading its large crevasses, to Camp Schurman at about 9,500 ft. From the camp go around the south side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Curtis, descend the Inter Glacier, and follow the Glacier Basin Trail out to White River. Starting from the Mowich Lake side needs a car left at White River. The route finding on the Emmons is the main hazard in poor visibility, so keep a track of the way up if you came that way, and stay roped.
hazards: Serac hazard threatening sections of the ridge
Steep ice/snow with exposure
Committing, remote north-side position

Crevassed glacier approach via the Carbon. Rainier's glaciers flow fast for their size, so crevasses open early, snow bridges are unreliable, and the line that worked last season may not exist this one — treat old beta as a starting point, not a route description.

waysIn.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park
waysIn.season: May-Jul; the road to Mowich Lake has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently on April 22, 2025, so this start cannot be reached by car
waysIn.notes:
From Mowich Lake, follow the trail roughly 3 miles to Spray Park, then climb the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. The ridge narrows above Observation Rock; continue along it until you find bivouac sites. High camp is normally somewhere between about 9,500 and 10,300 ft, at the point where Ptarmigan Ridge runs into the main cone below the Liberty Cap icefall. Higher camps are worth the extra carry because they let you look at the bergschrund and pick a line the evening before.

This is the shorter of the two approaches, and it is the one most parties would choose if the road cooperated. Since April 2025 the Mowich Lake road has had no public access, because the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge was closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers; this start is unavailable until that changes. Even before that, the summer-only road usually opened after the route came into condition.

The approach to high camp is normally split over two days.
hazards: Mowich Lake road has no public access since April 2025; this start is unavailable
Bergschrund crossing off the Mowich Glacier, conditions-dependent
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp; site camp outside the serac fall line
Loose rock descending from high camp onto the glacier; verglassed rock and water ice on the upper mixed ground
Crevasse fall crossing the Mowich or Winthrop glaciers; avalanche-prone approach slopes on the Mowich/Carbon side
Committing, remote position with a carry-over descent by the Emmons-Winthrop
waysIn.whyThisWay: Only if the Mowich Lake road reopens, for a shorter walk in; it needs a car shuttle to the White River end, since the usual descent comes out there.

waysIn.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and Curtis Ridge
waysIn.season: Available earlier in the season than the Mowich Lake road, at the cost of a much longer approach
waysIn.notes:
Follow the Glacier Basin trail from White River Campground and leave it for St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft), about 4 miles in. Descend onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west toward Curtis Ridge, holding elevation. Cross Curtis Ridge, cross the Carbon Glacier, then climb moderate snow slopes onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point, where there are good bivouac sites.

This is the long way around the north side of the mountain and it shares its first half with the Liberty Ridge approach. It usually implies a car shuttle or, more often, a carry-over with descent by the Emmons–Winthrop back to White River — which conveniently is also the standard descent from the route itself.
hazards: Serac discharge from Willis Wall on the traverse between Curtis Ridge and the Carbon
Crevasse fields on the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers; crossing the Carbon
Long committing traverse with no quick exit; much longer approach
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp
Bergschrund and upper mixed ground; verglassed rock and water ice late season
Carry-over descent by the Emmons-Winthrop through large crevasses

name: Tahoma Glacier
approach: From the Westside Road gate at Dry Creek Trailhead: Tahoma Creek Trail to the Wonderland Trail (~5,600 ft), then onto the southern side of the Tahoma Glacier. The Tahoma Creek Trail is closed — washed out, unmaintained and exposed to debris flows from the glacier — so the usual alternative is to walk the road to Round Pass and take the South Puyallup Trail to the Wonderland Trail, then go either south to Emerald Ridge or north to St Andrews Park and up the Puyallup Cleaver, dropping onto the glacier on a ramp near 9,600 ft below St Andrews Rock.
descent: Reverse the route, or descend toward the standard Disappointment Cleaver/Ingraham route and arrange a shuttle back to Westside Road; a documented recent trip logged about 8,770 ft of net descent loss over a 21.5-mile car-to-car itinerary starting from the Westside Road closure.
hazards: Complex crevasse navigation
Serac and icefall hazard in the 'Sickle'
Long, committing approach with route-finding

waysIn.name: Westside Road and Tahoma Creek to St Andrews Rock, then the Sickle
waysIn.season: Roughly May-Jul, best in June; a west aspect that holds firmer snow later into the morning than the south-side routes
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Westside Road gate at the Dry Creek trailhead near 2,900 ft. The road is gated to vehicles a few miles in because of repeated Tahoma Creek flooding and debris flows; the remainder is walked or biked, and has been for years. Plan the road as part of the climb.

From the gate, take the Tahoma Creek Trail up to the Wonderland Trail near 5,600 ft, then onto the southern side of the Tahoma Glacier. Camps are used near Emerald Ridge lower down and around 9,800-10,400 ft near St Andrews Rock.

The glacier is climbed with a series of diagonal traverses: zigzag the south side to about 7,200 ft, then traverse back and forth around 9,000-10,000 ft to get through crevasse bands, then into the Sickle and out onto the plateau near 12,600 ft.

Car-to-car this is a very long outing — a documented itinerary from the road closure ran about 21.5 miles.
hazards: Complex crevasse navigation with several bands that have to be traversed around
Serac and icefall hazard in and below the Sickle, with unavoidable run-out exposure on the traverse
A long road walk at both ends and a very long car-to-car day
Route-finding on a committing west-side approach with no maintained trail above 5,600 ft
Thin late-season snow bridges over the upper glacier

name: South Face / Redoubt Glacier
approach: Southeast via Depot Creek and Redoubt Glacier. International border crossing required (Canadian side). From Ouzel Lake, cross Depot Creek and scramble rock steps and slabs southwest of the lake onto the Redoubt Glacier.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb or rappel the exposed Class 4 section from the summit horn back through the cannonhole, downclimb the loose gully/chimney system, and traverse back beneath the flying buttress to regain the notch at the head of the glacier. Rope up again for the glacier descent, then retrace the rock steps and slabs down to Ouzel Lake camp and follow the Depot Creek climbers' path back past the falls to Monument 65 and the vehicle.
hazards: Crevasses and a bergschrund on the Redoubt Glacier, worse in late season or low-snow years
Loose, rockfall-prone gully/chimney system below the cannonhole
Rotten Skagit gneiss on the summit block — test every hold
Exposed, belayed Class 4 downclimb from the cannonhole to the summit horn
Slick boulders at the Depot Creek Falls crossing (fixed ropes in place, condition varies)
No reliable cell coverage; carry a PLB or satellite device
Long, partly unmaintained/overgrown approach trail with downed logs

name: East Slopes (via Airplane Lake)
approach: Drive to the White River Trailhead (also called the Indian Creek Trailhead) at the end of White River Road/FS-6400: from Leavenworth take US-2 west 15 miles to Coles Corner, turn onto SR-207 (Lake Wenatchee Highway) for 10.5 miles, then continue on White River Road/FS-6400 for a final 10 miles to the trailhead (2,300 ft). Follow the Indian Creek Trail north/west, crossing the White River at the trailhead and Indian Creek near its mouth, for roughly 4.5 miles. Near Airplane Creek, leave the maintained trail and bushwhack/scramble about 2,000 ft up to Airplane Lake (this leg runs 1.5-2 miles); from the lake, continue off-trail to the upper east slopes and summit via one of the three route options. Round trip is roughly 16 miles with about 5,300 ft of gain; a logged first-hand ascent recorded closer to 12 miles and 5,000 ft via a more direct Airplane Creek line, taking about 7.3 hours up and 4.4 hours down. From Airplane Lake, three lines reach the summit: the northeast ridge (working around a hidden, non-obvious cliff band north of the lake), a direct ascent of the clean upper east face slabs, or a looser steep-talus variation. Favoring the drainage about a quarter-mile downstream of Airplane Creek reportedly avoids the worst of the brush on the bushwhack in.
descent: Most parties descend the same way they went up. At least one party notes an alternate ridge-descent option off the summit as an alternative to retracing the ascent line; whichever way is chosen, time creek crossings on Indian Creek/the White River for morning (lower, easier water) rather than late afternoon, when snowmelt runoff makes fords more difficult.
hazards: Off-trail bushwhacking through devil's club, vine maple, and blowdown between the Indian Creek Trail and Airplane Lake, worsened by sections of burned/dead forest
Stream crossings of the White River and Indian Creek that get noticeably harder in the afternoon as snowmelt raises water levels
Hidden cliff bands north of Airplane Lake that complicate the northeast ridge approach and can cliff out unwary parties
Lingering snow on the upper east face/slopes into July (continuous above ~4,700 ft in one logged July ascent), requiring an ice axe and step-kicking skills
Loose rock and steep talus on some summit approach variations
Sheer northwest face — not a descent or bail option

waysIn.name: Indian Creek Trail and the Airplane Creek bushwhack to Airplane Lake
waysIn.season: Late July through September is the reliable window. In July expect snow from around 4,000 ft and continuous cover above 4,700 ft, which makes the upper slopes a snow climb and calls for an axe.
waysIn.notes: From the road-end trailhead above Lake Wenatchee, the Indian Creek Trail crosses the White River on a footbridge — which has washed out in past years, forcing a ford — and runs up the valley through old growth and sections of burned, dead forest. Somewhere near Airplane Creek you leave the maintained tread; nothing marks the departure and it is easy to lose in brush or fog. The bushwhack from there to the lake is the hard part of the day: roughly two thousand feet of gain through devil's club, vine maple and blowdown, made worse by the standing dead timber. Favouring the drainage about a quarter mile downstream of Airplane Creek reportedly avoids the worst of the brush. Snow cover typically begins around 4,000 ft and becomes continuous near 4,700 ft in early season, so step-kicking on firm snow is normal here into July. Airplane Lake is the last reliable water and the only sensible flat camp. Time the White River and Indian Creek crossings for the morning, when the water is lower.
hazards: off-trail bushwhacking through devil's club, vine maple and blowdown, worsened by burned standing timber
White River and Indian Creek crossings that get harder through the afternoon as snowmelt rises
hidden cliff bands north of Airplane Lake that can cliff out a party working toward the northeast ridge
lingering snow on the upper east slopes into July
loose rock and steep talus on some summit variations
a sheer northwest face that is not a descent or a bail option

name: South Slopes (Standard)
approach: Two realistic approach corridors exist, both multi-day: (1) North Fork Quinault side — from the North Fork Quinault Trailhead at the end of the North Shore Road (not the South Shore Road, which leads to Graves Creek and the East Fork instead), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail or the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail (via Three Lakes and Kimta Peak) to Low Divide, 16 miles one-way by the river trail and much farther by the ridge, then cross-country/climbers'-path to Seattle Meadows below the peak's south side. (2) Elwha side — from the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road to it is closed to vehicles at Madison Falls by a washout, adding about seven miles each way on foot or bike), follow the Elwha River Trail up the Elwha valley toward Elwha Basin/Low Divide (on the order of 20+ miles one-way), then leave trail to climb into Noyes Basin on the peak's northeast side. Either way, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp, with several thousand feet of trail gain before any scrambling begins. The Seattle Creek Basin approach, up from the North Fork Quinault side, follows the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, forcing a steep, brushy bushwhack up onto the Mt. Noyes-Mt. Seattle ridge — expect slow going in heavy brush low down.
descent: Descend the ascent line in reverse: downclimb the east ridge scramble back to the scree/talus on the east side, cross back over the connecting ridge, and descend the west-side scree to Seattle Meadows camp. The scree and talus are loose and unconsolidated in places, so downclimb carefully rather than trying to glissade or boot-ski except where lingering early-season snow makes it safe; rockfall onto parties below is a real concern on the looser sections.
hazards: Steep, brushy bushwhacking where the Seattle Creek drainage becomes too steep to climb directly
Loose scree and talus on both the west and east flanks, with rockfall risk onto parties below
Unbridged river/creek fords on the Elwha and North Fork Quinault approaches that can become dangerous after rain or during snowmelt
Extreme remoteness — multi-day approach from the nearest trailhead in either direction, with the NPS explicitly noting that emergency help is far away and frequently impossible to contact

waysIn.name: Low Divide and Seattle Meadows
waysIn.season: Late July to mid-September
waysIn.notes: Reached up the North Fork Quinault or by the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge primitive route past Three Lakes and Kimta Peak, or from the Elwha side. Two other lines come in through Noyes Basin and directly up Seattle Creek Basin. Whichever you pick, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp.
hazards: Unbridged river and creek fords on the North Fork Quinault approach that become dangerous after rain or in snowmelt
Multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp; emergency help far away and frequently impossible to contact
Steep, brushy bushwhacking where the Seattle Creek drainage steepens
Loose scree and talus on both flanks with rockfall onto parties below
Northeast aspect drops thousands of feet — stay off that side
Lingering snow into early summer

waysIn.name: Up the Elwha to Low Divide
waysIn.notes: The long northern way: follow the Elwha River trail up the whole valley past Hayes River and Chicago Camp, then climb to Low Divide. It takes several days, and a road walk or bike ride may be needed to reach the trailhead.
hazards: Elwha River trail is several days long; a road walk or bike ride is needed to reach the trailhead
Unbridged river and creek fords on the Elwha approach, dangerous after rain or in snowmelt
Wasps in the lower forest sections in late summer
Steep, brushy bushwhacking where the Seattle Creek drainage steepens
Loose scree and talus on both flanks with rockfall onto parties below; northeast aspect drops thousands of feet
Extreme remoteness; emergency help frequently impossible to contact
waysIn.whyThisWay: When coming from the north side or crossing the range on foot; it takes several days, so most parties prefer the shorter Quinault walk to Low Divide.

name: Fisher Chimneys
approach: Park at the Lake Ann Trailhead on the east side of SR 542 (Mount Baker Highway), about 1 mile below Artist Point. Follow Lake Ann Trail #600, which immediately loses roughly 700-800 ft over its first ~1.7 miles through heather and blueberry slopes (a minor creek crossing near the low point), then climbs back about 1,000 ft over the final ~1.3 miles of switchbacks to the broad saddle above Lake Ann (about 4 miles and ~4,900-5,000 ft from the car). Just past the saddle is an unsigned junction: the right fork drops to Lake Ann's campsites and outlet — the last reliable water before the climb — while the left fork is the climber's boot path for Fisher Chimneys. That path sidehills north below Shuksan's lower moraines, crossing talus and lingering snow tongues (often firm/icy in early morning through July — microspikes and an axe are worth carrying) to a dry fall that is scrambled (3rd class) to regain the zigzagging trail. Continue along the base of the cliff band to its far end, roughly 5 miles from the trailhead and near 6,000 ft, where the Fisher Chimneys begin: a broken, leftward-ascending line of 4th-class rock steps and heather ledges leading up to the Winnie Glacier. Most parties camp at the top of the Chimneys near the upper White Salmon Glacier (about 6,700-6,800 ft), or higher on the rock rib above Winnie's Slide (about 7,200 ft). Watch for rockfall on the talus traverse and within the chimneys themselves (helmet essential, especially below other parties), and expect route-finding difficulty threading the braided chimney ledge system, which is easy to overshoot in poor visibility.
descent: Reverse the ascent line in its entirety. From the true summit, downclimb the short 3rd/4th-class summit block to the head of the central gully, then descend via a mix of downclimbing and roughly two or three rappels off established stations — slung rock horns and existing fixed rings or webbing (inspect any tat before trusting it, and be ready to back it up) — to the base of the summit pyramid. A single 60m rope works and cuts down on exposed downclimbing. Traverse to Hell's Highway, a roughly 60m ramp of steep snow or alpine ice, and downclimb it (or make a short rappel) back onto the Upper Curtis Glacier, then reverse the glacier traverse to the top of Winnie's Slide. Winnie's Slide is a sustained, often icy snow/ice slope usually downclimbed facing-in with pickets for protection; parties uncomfortable downclimbing it will instead rig a picket rappel — but be aware pickets left by earlier parties are frequently pulled by whoever follows, so don't plan around finding gear in place. Re-enter the Fisher Chimneys at the bottom of Winnie's Slide: the upper chimneys are mostly downclimbable 3rd/4th class, but the lowest steps have fixed rappel anchors and are commonly rappelled rather than downclimbed. In total, expect somewhere between two and six rappels for the full summit-to-Lake Ann descent depending on snow coverage, season, and the party's comfort downclimbing exposed 4th class — four is a reasonable average trip. Below the chimneys, retrace the climber's path and Lake Ann Trail back to the car.
hazards: Rockfall in the Fisher Chimneys, worsened by climber traffic on the loose rock
Crevasses on the Lower and Upper Curtis Glaciers
Loose rock and multi-party crowding in the summit pyramid's central gully

waysIn.name: Lake Ann Trail #600 from SR 542
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Lake Ann trailhead on the east side of the Mount Baker Highway, roughly a mile below Artist Point. The trail goes down first — several hundred feet over its first mile and a half — before climbing back to the broad saddle above Lake Ann at roughly four miles.

Just past the saddle there is an unsigned fork. The right branch drops to the lake, the campsites and the outlet, which is the last easy water. The left branch is the climbers' boot path, and it is distinct and well trodden — a very obvious break heading east toward the mountain.

That path sidehills north beneath Shuksan's lower moraines, switchbacking and crossing two gullies over talus and lingering snow tongues, and becomes vague right where you need it most: just short of the first chimney. Parties typically reckon around six hours from the car to the high camp on or above the chimneys, and expect the snow tongues to be firm enough for microspikes and an axe in the early morning well into July.
hazards: rockfall inside the chimneys, especially with parties above
firm or icy snow tongues on the talus traverse before the sun hits
the route-finding itself — the boot path deliberately goes obscure right at the chimney entrance
several dead-end side paths ending at cliff edges

name: Hanging Glacier
approach: Note: the Hanging Glacier/North Face approach lies in the White Salmon Creek drainage, one valley west of Price Lake, rather than on the Nooksack/Ruth Creek side with which it is sometimes grouped. Drive the Mount Baker Highway to Glacier, WA and get a backcountry permit at the Glacier Public Service Center (required), then continue up the Salmon Ridge/Mount Baker Highway corridor to the small pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge site. Walk around the gate and follow the old road past the lodge site roughly a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. From there, with adequate snow cover, descend northeast off-trail to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier — this is where roped glacier travel typically begins, with crevasse hazard increasing through the season. Ascend the glacier and moraine to a bivy around 6,000–6,500 ft, below the first rock/ice barrier. From the bivy, traverse climber's left, above and across the hanging glacier that sits over Price Lake (visible below to the north-east) and beneath the upper hanging glacier tucked under the first rock barrier, to reach the base of the shoulder dividing the White Salmon and Price Glacier cirques (roughly 7,500–8,000 ft), where the technical climbing begins. Key hazards: brush/alder low in the White Salmon valley when the snowline has receded; open crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier; and, especially in early season, frequent avalanches shedding off the true North Face — parties are advised to stay right of it during the traverse rather than drifting left onto the face itself. An alternate approach used by some parties climbs the Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide to a bivy near the Upper Curtis Glacier, then descends about 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier and traverses the NW Rib to reach the base of the Hanging Glacier — an option from the standard Lake Ann/Fisher Chimneys trailhead rather than the White Salmon side.
descent: From the summit, most parties tie into the same descent used off Price Glacier and the standard Sulphide route: downclimb/rappel the summit pyramid's gully system (natural horn-and-sling anchors, occasionally pickets — typically 1–3 short rappels on a single 30–60 m rope, condition-dependent) down to Hell's Highway (a ~60 m steep snow/ice step) and onto the Sulphide/Upper Curtis Glacier. Because this route's trailhead (White Salmon Lodge) is on the same north side of the peak rather than at Baker Lake or Ruth Creek, many parties then reverse west from the Upper Curtis, dropping back over the shoulder and down through Winnie's Slide (occasionally a single ~30 m rappel if icy) toward the head of the White Salmon Glacier, then plunge-step the glacier back down past the bivy site and out the same valley to the White Salmon Lodge trailhead — avoiding the long Lake Ann/Baker Lake shuttle that Price Glacier and Fisher Chimneys parties face. Watch for opening crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier on the way down, weak snow bridges late in the season, and brush/alder in the lower valley once snow cover thins.
hazards: Large crevasses high on the route
General north-side serac/icefall exposure shared with neighboring Price and North Face routes
The Hanging Glacier is retreating and its terminus is increasingly broken/rocky, which can add rockfall/icefall risk versus older route descriptions

waysIn.name: White Salmon Creek from the old lodge site, up the White Salmon Glacier to the dividing shoulder
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Aug. Earlier the valley is snow-covered and simpler but the true North Face above you sheds avalanches; later the crevasses on the White Salmon are open and the lower valley is alder
waysIn.notes: Get the backcountry permit at the Glacier Public Service Center on the way in — it is required, not advisory. Then continue up the Mount Baker Highway to the pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge site, walk round the gate, and follow the old roadbed roughly a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. From the road-end, with adequate snow cover, drop northeast off-trail to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Roped travel usually begins at the toe, and the crevasse hazard grows through the season. Ascend glacier and moraine to a bivy below the first rock and ice barrier. Published bivy elevations for this route disagree by around a thousand feet — so the honest instruction is to camp at the rock outcrops on the eastern edge of the White Salmon, where the ridge meets the face, rather than at a number. The Hanging Glacier and North Face approach is in the White Salmon Creek drainage, one valley west of Price Lake — not on the Nooksack and Ruth Creek side of the mountain.
hazards: Frequent avalanches off the true North Face onto the traverse, worst in early season
Serac fall from the very active hanging glacier itself
Open crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier that grow through the season; roped travel from its toe
Brush and alder in the lower White Salmon valley once the snowline recedes
Traverse with no easy retreat once committed; moat between rock wall and glacier
Gate and old roadbed approach; bivy on the mountain

waysIn.name: Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide, then down the White Salmon Glacier to the base
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Aug, once the Lake Ann trail is out from under snow
waysIn.notes:
The alternative used by parties who would rather start from the standard trailhead than from the White Salmon roadbed: from the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR-542, climb the Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide to a bivy near the Upper Curtis Glacier, then descend about 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier and traverse the northwest rib to reach the foot of the Hanging Glacier.

It is longer in vertical terms because it climbs to a camp and then gives back a thousand feet, and it commits you to regaining that thousand feet on the way out if you return the same way. Its advantage is a maintained trail to a known camp instead of a valley bushwhack, and it does not require the White Salmon roadbed to be walkable.

No trailhead-to-base time is given for this variant; published figures for it vary too much to quote one.
hazards: About 1,000 ft descent to the base that must be regained on the return if reversed
Winnie's Slide, sometimes rappelled rather than downclimbed when icy
Crevasses on both the Lower Curtis and the White Salmon glaciers
Avalanche exposure from the true North Face during the traverse
Serac fall from the active hanging glacier; descent normally exits a different valley from the start
Maintained trail to the camp, but Fisher Chimneys are loose and route-finding-heavy
waysIn.whyThisWay: For parties who would rather use the maintained Lake Ann trail and a known camp than the White Salmon valley bushwhack, accepting a climb then a loss of about a thousand feet.

name: North Face
approach: Park near the White Salmon day-lodge area on SR 542 (White Salmon Road, FS 3075), just before the Mt. Baker Ski Area's White Salmon lodge. Hike the old road, then traverse brushy ('schwacky') slide-alder slopes to open terrain near 3,300 ft, and continue up to the 5,500 ft saddle at the base of the North Face - roughly 2-3 hours from the car.
descent: Climb over the summit and descend by Hell's Highway, the Upper Curtis Glacier, Winnie's Slide and the White Salmon Glacier back toward the ski area, rather than reversing the steep north face.
hazards: Avalanche/serac fall from the Hanging Glacier above the route
Crevasses that open as the face bares out through summer
Dense slide-alder brush on the approach
Snow-condition dependent - soft afternoon snow is dangerous on the sustained 40-50 degree face

waysIn.name: White Salmon Lodge road (standard)
waysIn.season: spring to early summer; needs snow cover
waysIn.notes:
Pull off at the old White Salmon lodge site on the Mount Baker Highway, walk around the gate, and follow the old road past the lodge for about a mile to where it finishes in an old clearcut.

What you do next depends entirely on snow cover, and getting this wrong is the single biggest time sink on the approach. With good cover, drop northeast off the clearcut down to White Salmon Creek and walk the valley toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier — pleasant going. Without good cover, do not descend into the valley at all: hold your elevation as you enter the clearcut and contour around instead, giving up height only where a rock band or a stream crossing forces it. The valley bottom without snow is slide alder and devil's club.

From the glacier area, the route continues up toward the shoulder at the foot of the face.
hazards: avalanches off the Hanging Glacier, which is very active and sweeps the approach terrain
slide alder and devil's club in the White Salmon valley once the snow has gone
unbridged stream crossings when contouring the low-snow variation
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier

waysIn.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
waysIn.season: winter/spring, on skis
waysIn.notes: An alternative used mainly by ski parties: start at the base of Chair 8 in the ski area and make a downhill traverse into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley, then climb over four thousand feet up the glacier. It removes the clearcut and the road walk at the cost of a long climb from the valley floor and a committing descent to start the day.
hazards: avalanche exposure from the Hanging Glacier across the whole basin
the initial descent commits you to regaining that height on the way out
waysIn.whyThisWay: In winter or spring on skis, when the road walk and clearcut are unattractive; start at the ski area and traverse down into the White Salmon valley.

name: Northwest Arete
approach: Two realistic approach options both start by parking at the lower White Salmon lodge on SR 542 (White Salmon Road, FR-3075) and following a dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile. The more direct option drops off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climbs to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area, then follows the ridgecrest to the base of the mountain's north side. The alternative continues up the road as far as it goes, then travels off-trail up the valley until open slopes allow access to the lower White Salmon Glacier. From there, gain the crest of the northwest arête itself -- a long, remote line combining bushwhacking, complex route-finding, runout and loose rock, moderate alpine ice, and extensive glacier travel.
descent: Descend the summit pyramid by its central gully on the south side, then follow the Fisher Chimneys descent: down Hell's Highway onto the Upper Curtis Glacier and across to the top of Winnie's Slide. Descend Winnie's Slide (steep snow, occasionally icy enough to rappel) to the head of the White Salmon Glacier, then go down the glacier as directly as the crevasses allow to the lower White Salmon Glacier and out the White Salmon Creek valley to the road. Expect open crevasses and weak snow bridges on the White Salmon late in the season, and brush in the lower valley once the snow is gone.
hazards: Staying on the arête crest is used deliberately to minimize icefall exposure from the glaciers on either side
Loose rock and route-finding difficulty on lower sections
Long, sustained route — bivying on route is considered undesirable

waysIn.name: White Salmon Creek roadbed, then the ridgecrest opposite the ski area
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. This is the more direct of the two options and it is a bushwhack, so it wants the ground clear rather than snow-covered
waysIn.notes:
Park at the lower White Salmon lodge on SR-542 (White Salmon Road, FR-3075) and follow the dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile. This first stretch is common to both options.

The direct option then drops off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climbs to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area, then follows that crest to the base of the mountain's north side.

This is a long Cascade adventure route rather than a line with a bootpack: bushwhacking, complex route-finding, runout and loose rock, moderate alpine ice, and extensive glacier travel, all in one day.
hazards: Bushwhacking with no tread, where a wrong drainage costs a day
Runout climbing on loose rock high on the arête
Moderate alpine ice and extensive glacier travel on the same outing as the rock
A very long day, with no good bivy on the crest
A descent that exits down the upper and lower White Salmon Glacier rather than reversing the climb

waysIn.name: Up the White Salmon valley to the lower glacier, then onto the crest
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The alternative from the same parking: continue up the road as far as it goes, then travel off-trail up the valley until open slopes allow access to the lower White Salmon Glacier, and gain the crest of the arête from there.

It trades the creek crossing and the direct climb to the crest for more valley travel and a glacier approach. Parties choosing between the two are choosing between bushwhack-then-ridge and valley-then-glacier; both are documented and neither is a shortcut.
hazards: Extensive glacier travel with crevasse hazard on the lower White Salmon
Off-trail valley travel with no tread and brush low down
