Loose rock and runout climbing on the arête above
Complex route-finding, one of the route's defining features
No quick retreat: the descent is a separate glacier descent, not a reverse of the climb
waysIn.whyThisWay: For parties who prefer a longer valley walk and a glacier approach to the crest over the brushy creek crossing and ridge climb of the other line.

name: Price Glacier
approach: Trailhead is the Nooksack Cirque Trail #750, reached via Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) off the Mount Baker Highway and then Nooksack Cirque Road (FS-34) to its end. The first obstacle is Ruth Creek itself, which has no bridge at the trailhead — cross on a large logjam/log crossing just downstream, then pick up the trail on the far bank at the registry box; in early summer or after rain the ford/log crossing can be unsafe and has turned parties back. From there follow the old roadbed about 2 miles through old growth to the original trailhead site, then continue along the North Fork Nooksack River — gravel bars when water is low, riparian brush-bashing when it's not — toward the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary (~3 mi in) and the North Cascades National Park boundary (~4 mi in). Rather than continuing all the way into the Nooksack Cirque proper, climbers heading for Price Glacier watch across the valley for the steep drainage of Price Creek, leave the maintained tread, cross the Nooksack on a log, and climb steeply up the forested hillside toward Price Lake — a sustained, open but steep forest slope, historically flagged, that takes roughly 1.5 hours from the river crossing to the lake basin (~4,700 ft). From the moraine below Price Lake, work up through cliff bands onto the heathery ridge on the lake's south side, then ascend slabs up and right to reach the first bivy sites on flat granite slabs around 6,000–6,500 ft, right at the glacier's margin. From bivy, rope up and traverse beneath Nooksack Tower — a notorious rockfall/icefall gully — to step onto the Price Glacier proper around 6,500 ft. Key hazards: the unbridged, sometimes-impassable Ruth Creek ford; sustained brush and route-finding along the Nooksack River flats; a steep, loose, flagged-but-unofficial climbers' path to Price Lake; and rockfall funneling through the gully between Nooksack Tower and the glacier's main lobe.
descent: The standard descent is NOT back to the Ruth Creek car — it's over the top and down the Fisher Chimneys to Lake Ann, a completely different trailhead. From the summit pyramid, downclimb and rappel the gully system on the pyramid's south side: climbers typically make 1–3 short rappels off natural anchors (slings on rock horns, occasionally pickets left in snow — don't count on finding a picket anchor still in place) on a single 60 m rope, which doubled through the anchor gives rappels of about 30 m, to drop through the soft or icy sections of the gully, though capable parties often downclimb the whole thing instead. This puts you on Hell's Highway, a ~60 m step of steep snow/alpine ice that accesses the Sulphide Glacier. Cross the Upper Curtis Glacier (watch for opening crevasses and weakening snow bridges by late summer) and downclimb Winnie's Slide, a short ice/snow step that some parties rappel (~30 m) when it's icy or the snow beneath is soft, to reach the top of the Fisher Chimneys. The Chimneys themselves (class 3–4) are generally downclimbed rather than rappelled. Continue down through the chimneys to Lake Ann and out the Lake Ann Trail to the Mount Baker Highway/Artist Point trailhead — roughly 13 miles of trail from where your car is parked at Ruth Creek, so plan a shuttle, hitch, or stashed bike. An alternative is to instead descend the Sulphide Glacier all the way down toward the Baker Lake/Shannon Ridge side — a non-technical glacier walk-off with no rappelling required — but that exits at yet another trailhead, again requiring a car shuttle. Ski parties sometimes reverse the Price Glacier itself (skiing the Price Headwall and the glacier's eastern lobe back to Price Lake), but that is a specialized, avalanche- and icefall-exposed line, not the climbers' descent.
hazards: Significant serac fall hazard - the icefall above the route has calved large blocks onto climbers' lines in past seasons
Rockfall from the Nooksack Tower side of the approach
Difficult, potentially un-crossable creek ford at the Ruth Creek trailhead in high water

Heavily crevassed — early season a deep snowpack bridges the large crevasses and bergschrunds, but by late season expect bare glacier ice and having to drop into and climb out of their overhanging sides. Condition reports for the current season matter more here than the grade.

waysIn.name: Nooksack Cirque Trail #750 via Hannegan Pass Road
waysIn.season: May-Jun; a heavy snowpack is preferred
waysIn.notes:
Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) off the Mount Baker Highway, then Nooksack Cirque Road (FS-34) to its end. There is no bridge over Ruth Creek at the trailhead — the crossing is on a large logjam a little downstream, and in high water or after rain it has turned parties around before they started.

Beyond the crossing the old roadbed runs about two miles through old growth to the original trailhead, then it is river-bottom travel along the North Fork Nooksack: gravel bars when the water is low, riparian brush when it is not. You pass the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary at roughly three miles and the national park boundary at about four.

Rather than continuing into the cirque, leave the tread and watch across the valley for the steep drainage of Price Creek. Cross the Nooksack on a log and climb the forested hillside toward Price Lake — steep, open forest with old flagging, about an hour and a half from the river to the lake basin at roughly 4,700 ft. Budget the better part of a day for the approach; most parties treat the whole climb as two to three days.
hazards: unbridged Ruth Creek log crossing, sometimes impassable
brush and vague route-finding along the river flats
steep, loose, unofficial climbers' path to Price Lake
rockfall and icefall down the gully between Nooksack Tower and the glacier's main lobe — large blocks reported

name: Sulphide Glacier
approach: From the end of FS Road 1152-014 (~2,500 ft), the route starts on the Shannon Ridge Trail #742, an old roadbed heading northeast. Follow it about 2 miles to where the road tread gives out around 3,800 ft, then continue on the true trail, angling left through brush onto the open ridge crest. Roughly 0.75 mile farther (~4,600 ft) the trail reaches timberline, where continuous snow often persists into midsummer (crampons/axe are worth carrying above this point in early season). From timberline, follow the broad, undulating ridge crest through meadows and broken timber for about 2 more miles to a pass where a major north-south ridge is met (~5,400 ft) — the Sulphide Glacier and the summit pyramid come into view here for the first time. From the pass, continue up open slopes and snow onto the glacier's toe; established bivy sites sit at roughly 6,200 ft (lower camp: several dry tent pads, composting toilet) and 6,500 ft (upper camp: dry pads, no reliable water). Total approach to high camp is roughly 4-5 miles one-way with about 3,500-4,000 ft of gain. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and ascend the broad, moderately crevassed Sulphide Glacier — crevasse hazard increases through the season as snow bridges thin, so carry and know how to use crevasse-rescue gear — angling climber's-left toward the base of the summit pyramid at roughly 8,400-8,500 ft. Water is unreliable above timberline late in the season; plan to melt snow at camp, and expect the first mile of brushy old road to be a bit overgrown and easy to lose in low light.
descent: Descend the same line: reverse the Sulphide Glacier back to camp, then the Shannon Ridge Trail back to the trailhead. Off the summit, the standard descent down the central gully of the summit pyramid is a mix of downclimbing and rappelling. NPS climbing rangers have reported parties periodically replacing worn rap rings and anchors in the gully, so expect a mix of fixed rings/webbing at established stations supplemented by natural anchors (slung horns) rather than bolted hardware throughout. Plan on roughly two to four rappels depending on snow coverage and season — more rock is exposed and more rappels are typically needed later in the season, while early-season snow often lets parties downclimb and plunge-step more and rappel less. A 60m rope reaches between all standard stations; a 30m works but requires linking some sections with downclimbing between anchors. Note that stations are generally spaced for ropes with normal stretch — thin static or RAD-line-style ropes may leave gaps that require short, unprotected downclimbs between anchors. When the gully is dry and snow-free (typically later in summer), some parties instead descend the Southeast Ridge (about 5.3 with selective route-finding, or 5.6-5.7 held strictly to the crest) as a scramble alternative that avoids rappelling — but this is sustained 4th- to mid-5th-class terrain, not a simple walk-off, and isn't always in condition. Once back on the Sulphide Glacier, re-rope for glacier travel and retrace the ascent track to camp, watching for softened or newly opened crevasses in the afternoon.
hazards: Increasingly open crevasses on the Sulphide Glacier as the season progresses
Blue ice sections appear August-September, requiring screws/pickets for protection
Weak, sun-softened snow bridges in the afternoon
Unreliable water at the lower bivy after early season

A bergschrund crosses the route on the upper Sulphide Glacier; straightforward on firm early-season snow but the crossing becomes trickier and more exposed as the glacier opens up through mid/late summer

Active rockfall (including human-sized rocks) near the bootpack around 5,400ft, reported noticeably worse in the afternoon as temperatures rise and snow loosens — aim to clear this section earlier in the day

waysIn.name: Shannon Ridge Trail #742 (standard)
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Drive Baker Lake Road (FR 11) north from SR 20 near milepost 82, then FR 1152, then the 1152-014 spur to its end. The spur is rough and rutted; high clearance is the sensible minimum. An overnight in the park needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, obtained in person at Marblemount or arranged in advance with the wilderness office.

The trail opens as an old roadbed running northeast. It stays easy for roughly the first two miles, then a long-standing blowdown belt makes for tedious weaving before the tread turns into a real trail and angles left through brush onto the open crest of Shannon Ridge.

Above treeline the ridge rolls along through meadow and scattered timber to a pass at about 5,400 ft, where a major north-south ridge is joined and the Sulphide Glacier with the summit pyramid behind it comes into view for the first time. One party logged roughly four and a half hours and about 2,800 ft of gain to this point. Camps are established on the glacier's lower flats at about 6,200 ft and higher at about 6,500 ft; both have had composting toilets, but the upper one has been closed when full, so carry blue bags. There is no reliable running water above timberline late in the season.
hazards: loose rock funnelled down the summit-pyramid gully, worst late season when the snow has melted out of it
moat between glacier and pyramid, which widens through the season
crevasses on the Sulphide as snow bridges thin after midsummer
blowdown belt on the lower trail is easy to lose in the dark
no reliable water above timberline

name: White Salmon Glacier
approach: From the small pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge on the Mount Baker Highway, walk around the gate and follow the old road past the lodge site for about a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow cover, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Without it, hold your height through the clearcut and contour, losing elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings, to stay out of the slide alder in the valley bottom. Bivy sites sit among the rock outcrops along the eastern edge of the glacier.
descent: Downclimb the glacier back through Hell's Highway, across Curtis Glacier, down Winnie's Slide, and out around the clearcut to the White Salmon pull-off.
hazards: Avalanches off the Hanging Glacier onto the approach/glacier.
Crevasses on Curtis and White Salmon Glaciers, worse late season.

waysIn.name: White Salmon Lodge road
waysIn.season: spring; snow cover strongly preferred
waysIn.notes: Small pull-off at the old White Salmon lodge on the Mount Baker Highway. Walk around the gate and take the old road past the lodge site for about a mile until it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the glacier. Without good snow, do NOT go down into the valley — hold your height entering the clearcut and contour, shedding elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings. This is the same decision that governs the North Face approach, and it is the difference between a walk and a fight with slide alder. Going south past Lake Ann and over Austin Pass is not the way parties reach the White Salmon Glacier; the drainage is entered from the White Salmon side of the highway.
hazards: avalanche off the Hanging Glacier across the approach basin
brush in the valley bottom without snow cover
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier
Winnie's Slide holds firm ice when it has melted back

waysIn.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
waysIn.season: winter/spring, on skis
waysIn.notes: From the base of Chair 8, traverse downhill into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley and then climb over four thousand feet to near the base of Hell's Highway at the top of the glacier. This is the ski-descent party's usual line in.
hazards: a committing descent at the start that must be reclimbed on the way out
Hanging Glacier avalanche debris across the valley
waysIn.whyThisWay: Winter or spring on skis, when a party planning a ski descent starts from the ski area base and traverses down into the creek valley rather than walking the old road.

name: Standard Scramble (Putvin Trail / Lake of the Angels approach)
approach: The standard-route trailhead is the Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of Hwy 101 and about 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake trailhead, at roughly 1,600 ft elevation. Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels, not Mildred or Flapjack Lakes - those serve neighboring Mount Cruiser/Mount Lena out of the North Fork Skokomish/Staircase side. From the trailhead, Putvin Trail #813 is unmaintained for its last ~1.6 miles but well-traveled and easy to follow when snow-free; the tread is notably steep and narrow with unstable footing in spots as it climbs through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles in, the trail breaks into the open, grassy Whitehorse Creek basin and continues up to Lake of the Angels (about 3.5 miles and roughly 3,400 ft of gain from the trailhead, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace), a scenic alpine lake sitting in a cirque below Mount Stone and the Skokomish massif - this is the last reliable water source and the standard camp for an overnight trip. From the lake, climb westerly up pleasant alpine/heather slopes to a broad 5,800-ft saddle at the northeastern end of Mount Skokomish. From the saddle, a boot path/way-trail contours south and southwest across scree, grass, and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn, before turning to climb the final scree/rock slopes to the summit ridge. Total round-trip stats commonly cited are roughly 9-12 miles and about 5,000-5,100 ft of gain, with climbing parties reporting 3.5-5 hours up. Hazards: the narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread; lingering steep snow and real avalanche exposure on the upper slopes well into summer (reports note hazard even in August/September); and notoriously rotten 'Olympic choss' rock and loose scree/talus on the upper mountain and summit block, which is the crux of the route more than any single technical move.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the summit scree/rock to the saddle, then back along the boot path traverse across scree/grass/rock benches around the south and east flanks to the 5,800-ft saddle above Lake of the Angels, down to the lake, and out the Putvin Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb - there is no rappelling anywhere on the standard scramble route. The main descent hazard is the same rotten rock and loose scree that makes the ascent tricky: downclimbing the exposed class 3 sections near the summit ridge crest is generally regarded as harder and more hazard-prone than climbing them, and parties should stay well left/south of the steeper cliffy drop-off noted on the north side of the upper mountain (contouring too far right/north near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous — cut west over the ridge instead). Watch for rockfall onto climbers below on the scree/talus sections, expect residual snow in the gullies and on the traverse into early summer (ice axe/crampons may be warranted), and budget real time for careful downclimbing rather than assuming a fast glissade-style descent - one party logged about 2.5 hours from summit back to the trailhead, but that was in good, snow-free conditions.
hazards: Notoriously rotten, loose rock ('Olympic choss') throughout every approach and the summit scramble - test holds
Steep snow-filled gullies below the summit saddle hold avalanche/sluffing potential well into summer (even August/September slides have been reported)
Unmaintained, brushy, easy-to-lose way-paths on the Mildred Lakes and Flapjack Lakes sides requiring off-trail navigation
Post-fire hazards (standing dead/burned trees, rockfall, landslides) in the Bear Gulch Fire closure area
Exposed 'hanging'/'fingertip traverse' section near the true summit on the standard route
Mountain goats near Lake of the Angels and the peak's base

waysIn.name: Putvin Trail to Lake of the Angels, then west to the saddle north of Point 5945
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and this peak holds avalanche-capable snow in its upper gullies later than most — slides have been reported in August and September
waysIn.notes: This is the standard approach to Mount Skokomish. The Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) is on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of US-101 and about 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake trailhead, at roughly 1,600 ft. The trail is unmaintained for its last stretch but well-travelled and easy to follow when snow-free — steep, narrow, unstable footing in places through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles it breaks into the open grassy Whitehorse Creek basin, then climbs to Lake of the Angels at about 4,850-4,920 ft, roughly 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft of gain, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace. That is the last reliable water and the standard camp.
hazards: Notoriously rotten, loose rock throughout the upper mountain and summit scramble — test holds
Steep snow-filled gullies below the summit saddle carry avalanche and sluffing potential well into summer, with August and September slides reported
An exposed hanging or fingertip traverse section near the true summit
Three summit horns, and a false one has fooled parties
The narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread, and the root-and-rock headwall on it
Mountain goats near Lake of the Angels and the peak's base

waysIn.name: Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the off-trail brush above the lakes is much easier with lingering snow cover
waysIn.notes: This is not the standard approach, but it is a real approach into the Skokomish-Cruiser-Lincoln group, and it is the usual way to Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln. From the Mildred Lakes trailhead on Hamma Hamma Road, the trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford Huckleberry Creek at about 2,000 ft near 1.4 miles — the last reliable water before the hard part, and easy to lose in poor light. It then gains roughly 1,000 ft in about half a mile on hand-and-foot root and rock ladders, one pitch near 75-80 degrees, to a ridge high point at about 4,100 ft near 2.5 miles. From the ridge the trail drops about 250 ft to Lower Mildred Lake and continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser at about 3,850 ft near 4.3 miles, with informal camps on rock benches and the last dependable water before going off-trail. Above the lakes the route leaves the lakeshore path entirely into slide-alder and heather bushwhacking that neighbouring-peak accounts describe as very brushy, climbing to an open basin and connecting saddle beneath Skokomish's south peak at about 5,500 ft.
hazards: Unmaintained, brushy, easy-to-lose way-paths above the lakes requiring off-trail navigation
Root and rock ladders on the approach trail, one pitch near vertical, dangerous when wet
Slide-alder bushwhacking that is far worse without snow cover
The same rotten upper-mountain rock and avalanche-capable gullies as the standard side
Post-fire hazards — standing dead and burned trees, rockfall and landslides — near the area burned by the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire
waysIn.whyThisWay: When combining the climb with Mount Cruiser or Mount Lincoln, or to avoid the steep Putvin trail; the brushy off-trail stretch above the lakes is easier with lingering snow.

name: Silver Glacier
approach: Two camp options are used. Via Silver Creek: arrange a Ross Lake Resort water taxi (reservation required) roughly 25 miles up Ross Lake to a drop-off at the Silver Creek mouth (1,600 ft); a trail climbs the north side of Silver Creek about 2.5 miles to an old cabin at 2,900 ft, after which the route continues cross-country (occasional blazes) across slide-alder and forest slopes to the Silver Lake basin camp (6,763 ft). Via Ouzel Lake: use the Depot Creek approach (see the Southwest Ridge route) to Ouzel Lake (5,700 ft), then climb toward and over the Custer-Spickard saddle. From Ouzel Lake, climb north-east from the lake's north side up the obvious wide gully to the 7,380-ft Custer-Spickard saddle and step onto the Silver Glacier beyond it. From Silver Lake there is no saddle to cross: walk round the north side of the lake to its south-west end, then south across moraine and snow, skirting a small buttress, to the glacier toe at about 7,400 ft.
descent: From the summit, down-climb the short Class 4 step to the sub-summit notch (~8,500 ft), re-cross the Silver Glacier (roping up as on the ascent) back down through its flat section to about 7,400 ft, then either return to the Custer-Spickard saddle (7,380 ft) and descend the wide gully to camp at Ouzel Lake, or drop north from the glacier toe over moraine and round the lake to camp at Silver Lake. No fixed rappel anchors are documented; downclimbing/glacier travel is standard.
hazards: The Silver Glacier, like most North Cascades glaciers, is thinning over time, so crevasse patterns and the safest line shift from year to year.
The summit-block step is rated Class 4 on loose, lichen-covered rock.
Reaching the Silver Lake camp via Silver Creek depends on a reservable, non-scheduled water taxi from Ross Lake Resort.

waysIn.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
waysIn.season: Late July through September
waysIn.notes: Book a water taxi for the long run up Ross Lake and get dropped at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft; above that the route is cross-country with occasional blazes, across slide alder and forest slopes, to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft. This is the shorter side for this particular route and it keeps the whole trip inside the United States, at the cost of depending on a boat.
hazards: Boat access from Ross Lake Resort must be booked; no road out if plans slip
Slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin at 2,900 ft
Loose moraine between the lake and the glacier toe
Crevasses and a bergschrund on the Silver Glacier; the glacier is thinning so lines shift yearly
Class 4 summit-block step on loose, lichen-covered rock
Long, committing retreat from a high camp

waysIn.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
waysIn.season: Late July through September, and only with passports
waysIn.notes: The other way in starts on the Canadian side: a rough spur off the lake road to a washout at about 2,600 ft, an overgrown roadbed to the boundary obelisk and register, and then the climbers' path up the creek through old growth to the falls, whose wet slabs and old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in. Above them the path leads to the lake camp at about 5,700 ft. From that camp the way to this route climbs toward and over the col between the two peaks rather than onto the south-west side.
hazards: International border crossing on foot; passports needed
Wet slabs and an old fixed hand-line at Depot Creek Falls, the crux of the walk-in
Overgrown approach road that washes out and lengthens the walk
Crevasses and a bergschrund on the Silver Glacier beyond the Custer-Spickard saddle
Class 4 summit-block step on loose, lichen-covered rock
Taking the wrong route from the shared Ouzel Lake camp costs a day
waysIn.whyThisWay: Usually the shortest way, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

name: Southwest Route / Silver Lake
approach: From the Depot Creek Road washout (~2,600 ft, reached via a rough 4WD spur off Chilliwack Lake Road out of Chilliwack Lake Provincial Park, BC), the hike-in starts on the old roadbed: walk it about 9 minutes to an inconspicuous spur road on the left, follow that spur roughly 4 minutes to a T-junction, then bear right onto an extremely overgrown, sporadically muddy road for about 35 minutes to Monument 65 at the US-Canada border (roughly 45 minutes/0.8 hr total from the washout). From the border the route becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path following Depot Creek through beautiful old-growth forest - easy going where deadfall has been cut out, though dozens of uncut logs remain to step over in places. About 3 miles in, the path reaches Depot Creek Falls, the approach's real crux: crossing wet, slick boulders and slabs at the base of the falls. An old fixed hand-line was still serviceable as of a 2017 NPS trip report and assists at the vertical step here, but it should be treated with caution and backed up if in doubt - this is the approach's primary hazard, especially with a pack on wet rock. Above the falls the path continues through Depot Creek Meadow and Upper Depot Creek to Ouzel (Silver) Lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat, sandy, mostly treeless benches that serve as the standard base camp for both Spickard and neighboring Mount Redoubt, about 5-6 miles and roughly 6 hours of hiking from the road-end washout; Depot Creek and Ouzel Lake itself provide reliable water throughout. From camp, gain the climbing route by ascending a broad talus couloir and stream drainage north/northeast toward the ~7,200 ft Silver Lake saddle; well before the actual pass, cut right around the toe of a steep rocky buttress into open heather-and-moraine basins and traverse to the toe of the Southwest Glacier, roughly 2.5 hours above camp. Rope up and don crampons/crevasse gear here: the glacier's climber's-right margin offers a line of hard 30-40 degree snow/ice with relatively few crevasses, but roughly halfway up, one distinctly 'inhospitable-looking' crevasse must be crossed on a marginal snowbridge - probe it carefully and be prepared for the bridge to have deteriorated depending on the season. A short, steep, loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on the ~8,000 ft col on Spickard's southwest ridge, the start of the summit scramble (easy 3rd-class rock and up to ~35-40 degree snow to the summit ridge). In early July a ditch cut across the road about a mile short of the trail start can stop low-clearance cars; budget extra walking if you cannot cross it.
descent: The standard descent simply reverses the ascent line - there is no separate descent route and no rappelling on the Southwest Route. From the summit, downclimb the short scree chute and traverse back across to the east side of the crest, then reverse the short section of Class 2-3 gullies, chimneys, and rock ribs down to the notch/col on the southwest ridge. From the col, downclimb the short, steep, loose rock step back onto the head of the Southwest Glacier and re-rope for glacier travel. Descend the same climber's-right line of 30-40 degree snow/ice, re-crossing (or finding an alternate line around) the marginal snowbridge over the mid-glacier crevasse encountered on the way up - glacier conditions and bridge integrity can change meaningfully between morning ascent and afternoon descent, so reassess rather than assuming the same line is safe. Off the glacier, reverse the traverse across heather and moraine slopes and descend the talus couloir/stream drainage back to Ouzel Lake camp; from there, retrace Depot Creek trail (re-crossing at Depot Creek Falls via the fixed hand-line) back to the Depot Creek Road washout. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent: no fixed rappel anchors exist anywhere on the route per every trip report reviewed - the rope carried is solely for glacier travel and crevasse rescue, not rappelling. The steep, loose rock in the summit gullies and at the glacier-head gully step is the main descent-specific hazard; a party could choose to belay or hand-line a member down the loosest short step near the col if conditions or skill warrant, but this is not standard practice and no such anchor is established.
hazards: Crevasses on the Southwest Glacier, including a marginal snow bridge that persists in most seasons
Loose, sharp rock on the final Class 2-3 gullies, chimneys, and ribs near the summit
Slick, spray-soaked rock at the Depot Creek Falls crossing, aided by aging fixed hand-lines
Devil's club and slide alder brush hiding uneven footing on the lower approach
Extreme remoteness and lack of cell coverage complicating any self-rescue or evacuation

waysIn.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
waysIn.season: Late July through September, for a crossable glacier and a passable creek
waysIn.notes:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.
hazards: Border crossing on foot; passport needed, with a register at the obelisk
Washed-out road lengthens the walk without warning
Wet slick boulders and slabs at Depot Creek Falls with an old fixed hand-line of unknown condition
Crevasses on the southwest glacier, including a marginal snow bridge on the standard line
Short steep loose rock gully at the glacier head, then loose Class 2-3 ribs and gullies near the summit
30-40 degree snow near the summit ridge
Extreme remoteness, no cell coverage
waysIn.whyThisWay: Usually the shortest way, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

waysIn.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
waysIn.season: Late July through September, once the boat is running and the cross-country is clear of snow
waysIn.notes:
The other side of the mountain is reached without leaving the United States. A booked water taxi runs a long way up Ross Lake to a drop at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek for roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft, above which the way is cross-country with occasional blazes across slide alder and forest slopes to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft.

This puts you on the opposite side of the peak from the Depot Creek camp, so it changes which col you reach and in what order - plan the climb from this camp rather than translating a description written from the other one.
hazards: Boat access must be booked; no road out
Slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin at 2,900 ft
Long carry to a high camp at about 6,763 ft
Crevasses on the glaciers either side of the divide, including a marginal snow bridge on the southwest glacier
Short steep loose rock gully at the glacier head and loose Class 2-3 rock near the summit
Camp is on the opposite side from Depot Creek, so col-based descriptions can mislead

name: Monitor Ridge
approach: From the Climbers Bivouac trailhead (3,700 ft, the highest vehicle access on this side of the mountain, reached via FR-90/FR-83/FR-81/FR-830 from Cougar), the route starts on the signed Ptarmigan Trail #216A through open forest. This trail climbs a moderate 1,100 ft over about 2.25 miles to timberline at roughly 4,800 ft — the last shade and the last practical spot to filter water (a couple of small seasonal creeklets cross the lower trail; nothing reliable higher up, so most parties carry all water from the car). At timberline the trail ends and the route transitions onto the open volcanic slopes of Monitor Ridge itself: a broad rib of old lava flows flanked by loose pumice and ash. From here to about 7,000 ft the route is marked by a line of large wooden posts spaced across the rock — in fog or whiteout, losing these posts is the single biggest route-finding hazard on the climb, since a minor drift off-line can put you on steep, loose, off-route terrain. Above 7,000 ft (roughly the last 1,300 ft to the crater rim) the posts end and the climb becomes an unmarked scramble/boot-pack up steep, loose pumice, ash, and scattered rock — two steps up, one slide back is typical, and it's more efficient on the rock ribs of the ridge than in the ash gullies beside them. A Washington-permit (year-round, required above 4,800 ft) is checked at or near the trailhead. There is no technical climbing on this route — it is a long, steep hike/scramble — but full winter conditions (ice axe, crampons, and avalanche awareness on the upper slopes) can apply well into late spring.
descent: Descent is the same Monitor Ridge line back to timberline and then the Ptarmigan Trail back to Climbers Bivouac — there is no rappelling on this route (0 rappels; it is entirely a walk-off/scramble descent). The critical descent hazard is at the top: the crater rim is corniced with wind-built overhanging snow/ice that has repeatedly broken away, including a fatal collapse and multiple large rim failures in recent years, so the Forest Service and USGS explicitly warn to stay back at least 30 ft (9 m) from the visible rim edge and never approach or stand on a cornice for the crater view. From the true summit, descend back to the false summit and pick up the wood-post line down through the loose pumice/ash upper slopes; below about 7,000 ft the marked posts guide you back toward timberline, but climbers should double-check they're following the correct post line on the way down, since it's easy to wander onto a neighboring, unmarked drainage in poor visibility. Depending on season and snow coverage, glissading is possible on sections of the upper mountain and can significantly speed the descent, but chutes are frequently thin, rocky, and mixed with bare ash/pumice patches later in the season, so glissading should be assessed conservatively (an ice axe for self-arrest is standard kit). Below timberline, follow Ptarmigan Trail #216A back down through the forest to the Climbers Bivouac parking lot.
hazards: Cornice collapse at the crater rim — stay 30+ ft back from the visible edge
Glissading falls without self-arrest — FS-cited leading cause of climber injury
Loose pumice, ash, and boulder rockfall on the unmarked upper 1,300 ft
Whiteout/lost-descent into the wrong drainage off the broad summit dome
Altitude sickness possible above ~6,500 ft
Active volcano — unpredictable volcanic hazard (steam/gas, unrest) with no warning

waysIn.name: Climbers Bivouac and the Ptarmigan Trail to the marked ridge
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Oct for the summer route; full winter conditions with ice axe and crampons can apply well into late spring
waysIn.notes:
From the Climbers Bivouac trailhead at about 3,700 ft — the highest vehicle access on this side of the mountain — start on the signed Ptarmigan Trail #216A through open forest. It climbs a moderate 1,100 ft over about 2.25 miles to timberline near 4,800 ft. That is the last shade and the last practical water; a couple of small seasonal creeklets cross the lower trail and nothing is reliable above, so most parties carry everything from the car.

At timberline the trail ends and the route moves onto the open volcanic slopes of Monitor Ridge itself: a broad rib of old lava flows flanked by loose pumice and ash.

A permit is required above 4,800 ft year-round and is checked at or near the trailhead.

There is no technical climbing here. It is a long, steep hike and scramble, and the difficulty is navigation and footing rather than terrain.
hazards: Losing the wooden posts in fog or whiteout, which puts parties onto steep loose off-route ground
Unstable cornices and fall-through risk at the crater rim
Deep loose pumice and ash above 7,000 ft with poor footing in both directions
No water above the lower trail
Full winter conditions and avalanche terrain on the upper slopes well into late spring

name: Standard Scramble (Marmot Lake / Duckabush approach)
approach: Start at the Duckabush Trailhead (FR 2510-060) off US 101 and follow the Duckabush River Trail #803. The first real test is Big Hump at mile 3.9: a steep, loose-rock push of about 1,000 ft in roughly 30 switchbacks, then a 800 ft drop back down to river level on the far side — this is the trail's technical crux underfoot, not the summit. Continue upriver through old growth and a burned section (standing dead snags — use caution in wind) to Five Mile Camp (5.3 mi), a popular water stop and camp at a set of rapids. Between the Olympic National Park boundary (~6.2 mi from the trailhead) and Ten Mile Camp expect scattered blowdown and a documented trail washout that must be scrambled around rather than crossed directly. Above Duckabush Camp (about mile 17.7), the trail fords the Duckabush River itself — a wide crossing that can run thigh-deep and swift in early season or after rain; scout upstream/downstream for the best braid and use a pole. From Duckabush Camp, continue upvalley roughly 3 more miles on the Duckabush/O'Neil Pass trail; the unmarked Marmot Lake climbers' route then leaves the maintained trail (no sign, occasional cairns at best) and follows a small feeder creek up climber's-left into a rocky amphitheater on the west side of Mount Steel's summit. This final stretch is cross-country travel over heather benches and talus, finishing on easy Class 2 slopes to the summit ridge and the 6,225-ft high point. Snow lingers in the amphitheater and on the upper slopes into summer, with nasty cornices reported on the summit ridge until late June, so carry an ice axe and expect firm early-morning snow before roughly early July. Water is reliable along the Duckabush and at Marmot Lake but scarce once you leave the creek for the amphitheater, so top off there. With Marmot Lake itself over 21 miles from the trailhead, this route is done as a multi-day backpack with a high camp at Marmot Lake or the amphitheater, not a car-to-car day climb. A second, reportedly easier approach starts from First Divide (13-14 miles from the Staircase trailhead via the North Fork Skokomish Trail): follow the ridge west into a basin holding an unnamed lake, drop southwest to the saddle between Mount Steel's two summit humps, then finish north along the summit ridge; this line shares the same early-summer cornice/avalanche caution near the ridge crest. That approach is closed: the park lists the North Fork Skokomish Trail from Staircase to First Divide, and First Divide camp, as closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on its trail-conditions page (updated September 14, 2026) or fire-conditions page (updated September 18, 2026).
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly: downclimb the Class 2 talus/heather slopes and any lingering snow back through the amphitheater to the feeder creek, rejoin the Duckabush/O'Neil Pass trail, and retrace Trail #803 the full distance to the trailhead. This is a non-technical scramble route with no established rappel stations and no rock protection reported on any route description found — no rappelling is required; treat any steep snow patches with an ice axe/self-arrest rather than a rope. The two real hazards on the way out are the Duckabush ford just above Duckabush Camp (worse in the afternoon with elevated snowmelt flow than on an early-morning crossing) and the loose, steep switchbacks of Big Hump on tired legs — most parties split the roughly 21+ mile walk-out with a second night at Five Mile Camp or Ten Mile Camp rather than pushing straight through.
hazards: Cornices and steep, unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge/approach gullies persisting into late June
Avalanche potential on the east-facing slopes below the summit in early season
Long, unmarked off-trail travel above the amphitheater — easy to lose the line in fog or low visibility
Fallen timber in burned sections of the lower Duckabush valley
Untreated water carries giardia risk; treat all sources
Extremely remote setting — any rescue response will likely take a full day or more

waysIn.name: Duckabush River Trail to the unmarked creek turnoff
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Twenty-odd miles up the Duckabush over Big Hump, with a wide ford of the river above Duckabush Camp that runs thigh-deep and swift in early season. The climbers' line leaves the maintained trail roughly three miles below Marmot Lake. A multi-day backpack with a high camp at the lake or in the basin, never a car-to-car day.
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
Unmarked turnoff and unmapped off-trail travel above the amphitheater, easy to lose in fog
Wide Duckabush River ford above Duckabush Camp, thigh-deep and swift early season or after rain
Fallen timber and standing dead snags in the burned sections of the lower valley
Steep loose switchbacks on Big Hump, hard on tired legs
Extremely remote, rescue likely takes a day or more

waysIn.name: First Divide and the unnamed lake basin
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Parties generally find this the easier of the two lines and it is much shorter, but the corridor on that side has been closed by fire damage — confirm before planning around it. From the divide the route runs west into a basin, then over a col and north along the crest.
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June; stay back from the eastern lip
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall on the closed valley corridor
Open basin ground that is easy to lose in fog
Loose talus on slopes either side of the col
Approach corridor closed since the fire, so access is not currently available
Turning the wrong way off the saddle commits you to a different peak
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the North Fork Skokomish corridor is open: it is far shorter and easier than the Duckabush walk, but fire damage has closed the trail, so check status first.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the gate on Olney Creek Road (the drive-in ends here, at roughly 1,700 ft, since the road has been closed to public vehicle travel), the route starts as a road-walk. Follow the closed logging road uphill for about 4.8 miles, past a first switchback and on to a second switchback where the grade eases around 3,700 ft — this is the key junction. Leave the road here and pick up an unsigned but well-established climbers' path on the right (north) side, which climbs onto and follows a forest ridge crest. The path fades out around 4,050-4,200 ft; from that point, leave any tread and traverse southeast cross-country, aiming for a small pond just northeast of point 4875, then continue southeast to a second minor ridge. Cross open slopes on this ridge into the rocky basin holding One Acre Lake (roughly 6 miles and ~3,000 ft of gain from the road gate/Sultan Basin Road) — this is the last reliable water source and a common camp for parties splitting the trip over two days. From the lake, work up and around toward the base of the prominent summit block, aiming for the bowl directly below it. The final approach pitch is a steep slope/gully leading to the notch just below the summit ridge; expect a mix of dirt, talus, and (in early season) snow, with the gully becoming genuinely difficult — muddy, loose, and exposed — once it melts out in mid-to-late summer. Route-finding through the mid-mountain traverse (road-walk to ridge path to cross-country bench) is the crux of the approach itself and is easy to lose in fog or on a first visit; the mapped road alignment is reportedly inaccurate here, so trust the on-the-ground second-switchback landmark over the map. Winter and spring ascents cross at least one avalanche-prone slope below the summit bowl — one trip report noted watching roughly 20 slides release nearby during a single outing, so avoid this line in or after a storm cycle or during rapid warming.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: back across the short exposed ridge section from the summit hump, then down through the notch and back into the steep summit gully. In dry, snow-free conditions most parties downclimb the gully directly (it's an easy-4th-class scramble on dirt and rock), then reverse the cross-country traverse past the pond near point 4875 back to the climbers' path, and follow that path and the closed road back down to the gate. This is a walk-off/downclimb for competent scramblers in good conditions — no rappelling is strictly required. That said, the gully is frequently wet, muddy, and loose, and parties uncomfortable downclimbing exposed 4th class on that surface commonly opt to rappel it instead; there are at least a few natural anchor options (slings around trees/rock horns, including one built around a mountain hemlock) near the top of the gully, consistent with a single short rappel of roughly 50-60 feet to get past the steepest, most exposed section — a single 30m/60m rope is more than sufficient either doubled or as a single strand. These are backcountry natural anchors, not bolted or fixed hardware, so carry your own webbing/cord and rap rings, and back up any tat you find before trusting it. In winter conditions, most parties rope up for the gully on the way down (not just up) given the exposure, and cornices can form along the summit ridge — the guidance from trip reports is to stay climbers' right on the ridge and rig a hand line if anyone in the party is uncomfortable, since cornices can look like solid ground but are not. Below the gully, the descent hazards mirror the approach: avalanche exposure on the summit bowl slopes in winter/spring, and easy-to-lose route-finding through the unmarked ridge-path-to-road transition around 3,700-4,200 ft, especially in whiteout or at dusk.
hazards: Short, steep, exposed 4th class gully near the summit — loose rock, often wet/muddy, the main technical crux
Dense brush (slide alder, devil's club) on the lower approach off-trail sections
Cornices and avalanche terrain in and above the summit gully during winter/spring ascents
Unreliable/changing road-gate status on Olney Creek Road, which can add unplanned miles and elevation gain to the day
Inaccurate mapped road alignment near Olney Creek — parties note the drawn road doesn't match the road on the ground

waysIn.name: Olney Creek Road gate, the closed logging road and One Acre Lake
waysIn.season: July through September once the gully has melted out and the lower brush has died back. The gully holds snow and ice into June, and it refreezes with the first fall storms. It is also climbed as a snow route in winter and spring, when parties rope up for the final pitch and manage cornice and avalanche hazard.
waysIn.notes: The drive ends at the gate where Olney Creek Road leaves the Sultan Basin Road, and the day starts on foot up the closed roadbed. Walk the road uphill for about 4.8 miles, past a first switchback and on to a second one where the grade noticeably eases around 3,700 ft — that second switchback is the key junction and there is nothing signed about it. Mapped road alignments in this area are known to be wrong, so trust the switchback you can see on the ground over the line drawn on a map. Leave the road there and pick up an unsigned but well-established boot path on the right, north side, which climbs onto a forest ridge crest and follows it. The path fades out somewhere around 4,050 to 4,200 ft; from there leave any tread and traverse southeast cross-country, aiming for a small pond just northeast of point 4875, then continue southeast to a second minor ridge and cross open slopes into the rocky basin holding One Acre Lake. Pass the lake on its east side, follow the drainage above it to a cluster of small tarns, and then work up and around toward the bowl directly beneath the summit block. This mid-mountain sequence — road to ridge path to cross-country bench — is the crux of the walk-in and is easy to lose in fog or on a first visit.
hazards: a short, steep, exposed fourth-class gully near the summit — loose, often wet and muddy, and the real crux
at least one avalanche-prone slope below the summit bowl in winter and spring
cornices along the summit ridge that can look like solid ground
dense slide alder and devil's club on the lower off-trail sections
an unreliable gate status on the access road that can add unplanned miles
mapped road alignments that do not match the road on the ground

name: South Route via Lake of the Angels
approach: From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25, ~1,600 ft), the Putvin Trail (#813) is a steep, primitive trail, unmaintained in its upper reaches, that climbs steeply and directly from the start — expect root-staircase steps and a boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. About halfway up, the trail meets a rock headwall that requires hand-over-hand climbing; a large tree root serves as the key handhold, and on at least one especially steep pitch a fixed handline rope has historically been in place to assist. Above the headwall the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet before reaching Lake of the Angels (~4,850 ft) in a dramatic cirque below Mt. Stone's south face and the St. Peter's Gate notch — about 3 miles and roughly 3,000 ft of gain from the road. There is little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake, and expect the trail to be slick when wet and to hold snow on shaded steps into early summer. From the lake, contour/climb toward St. Peter's Gate; just before the gate, turn sharply left and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in Mt. Stone's west ridge. Turn right at the notch and climb directly toward it, arriving at a first sub-summit rock; climb a short, low-Class-3 chimney to its top, cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a groove in the rock on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the summit. The route is Class 3, with a few moves on the summit block that some parties rate Class 4; from Lake of the Angels camp, figure roughly 2.5 hours up to the summit.
descent: Descend by reversing the same west-ridge/south-face scramble line back through the summit groove, exposed ridge, and chimney to the notch, then retrace the cliff-base traverse back to Lake of the Angels — allow roughly 1.5 hours summit-to-camp. From Lake of the Angels, descend the Putvin Trail the way you came: the rock headwall (tree-root handhold, sometimes a fixed handline) and the trail's many steep, loose, root-braided sections are noticeably harder on tired legs headed downhill — face-in downclimbing at the headwall and trekking poles on the lower switchbacks are both recommended. This is a walk-off/scramble descent on the standard route; no rappelling is required anywhere on the climb or the trail, and no fixed rappel anchors exist on this line.
hazards: Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels
Near-vertical, root/rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail
Loose rock on the headwall and summit block (rockfall risk to parties below)
Ambiguous class 3/4 crux near the summit

waysIn.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the basin above the lake well into summer
waysIn.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.
hazards: Near-vertical root and rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail, slick when wet and worse descending
Rock headwall mid-trail needing hand-over-hand moves, sometimes a fixed handline
Little to no reliable water on the lower trail
Snow lingering on shaded steps and in the basin above the lake into summer
Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels; fog common and parties lose the route
Loose rock on the summit block with rockfall onto parties below
Ambiguous Class 3/4 crux and exposed unprotected summit block

waysIn.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
waysIn.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.
hazards: Long off-trail route over multiple passes and basins with faint tread
Loose glacial moraine and exposed dirt-and-mud slopes near St. Peter's Gate
No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass
Fog on the upper mountain; parties have lost the route
Very long approach with limited bail options
Loose rock on the summit block and an ambiguous Class 3/4 crux
Exposed unprotected summit block
waysIn.whyThisWay: For a scenic two- or three-day trip through lake country, or to finish with a Lena Lake exit; slower and needs off-trail route-finding, so not the quick way up.

name: Cascadian Couloir
approach: Drive to the Esmeralda (DeRoux Campground/Teanaway) trailhead at the end of North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), elevation ~4,243 ft — from I-90 exit 85 near Cle Elum, take SR 970 northeast, then Teanaway River Road roughly 23 miles to the road-end parking. From the trailhead, hike an old mining road/climbers' trail about 0.25 mile to a fork and take the right (east) branch toward Longs Pass. The trail climbs a mostly open, sun-exposed hillside — worth starting before dawn in summer to avoid the heat — gaining roughly 2,000 ft over about 2 miles to Longs Pass (~6,250 ft), the high point of the approach and the first place Mount Stuart and the Cascadian Couloir come into view. From the pass, descend the steep, loose scree on the far side, dropping about 1,200-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek. Cross the creek on a log footbridge, then follow the Ingalls Creek Trail east for about a mile to a meadow and campsite area around 4,800 ft (good camps are found straight south of the couloir's outlet, and a few more near the footlog); this is the standard basecamp for an overnight ascent, though the route is also done car-to-car. From camp, pick up the climbers' trail up through the meadow to the toe of the couloir and begin ascending. Water is reliable at Ingalls Creek and in the meadow below the couloir but is not available higher up, so fill bottles before starting the climb. Trailhead-to-camp runs roughly 3-4 hours; camp-to-summit another 5-8 hours. The Ingalls Creek crossing can run high and fast in early-season snowmelt, and the Longs Pass hillside carries some avalanche exposure in winter/spring conditions.
descent: Standard descent is simply reversing the ascent line — a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling (0 rappels). From the false summit (~9,200 ft), descend the broken class 2-3 ridge back to the couloir, then work down the Cascadian Couloir itself, staying on the established climber's-left talus path around the permanent snowfield near 8,800 ft (parties who wander onto the right side of the snowfield have encountered old rappel-station remnants and much harder, more hazardous downclimbing — avoid this line). The couloir is notoriously loose top to bottom — sand, scree, and unstable blocks create real rockfall risk for parties below, and the upper sections splinter into a maze of use-trails and cairns that make route-finding genuinely tricky, especially at dawn/dusk or in whiteout; a GPS track or careful attention to your ascent line is worthwhile. An ice axe (and crampons in early season, or on any lingering snow tongue) should be carried for the descent through at least mid-summer. Continue down to Ingalls Creek, re-cross the footlog, and regain about 1,400-1,500 ft back up to Longs Pass over roughly 2-3 miles before descending the final stretch to the Esmeralda trailhead. Budget roughly 5-8 hours summit-to-car for this descent; it is also the standard descent for other Mount Stuart routes (e.g., the North Ridge) whose parties finish on the opposite side of the mountain from where they started.
hazards: Rockfall — loose rock, sand and scree in the couloir funnel debris onto lower climbers; helmets are considered mandatory and an early alpine start is strongly recommended to be off the couloir before the sun loosens rock.
Steep snow in the couloir in early season (into June) requiring ice axe and crampons and posing a slide/glissade-runout hazard.
The false summit (~9,200 ft) is not the true summit — the final stretch east along the ridge to the actual high point is exposed Class 2-3 scrambling.

Consistently loose rock/sand/scree throughout, worse in the upper couloir below the false summit (steeper, larger blocks); the funnel shape creates rockfall risk between ascending and descending parties -- helmets strongly advised
Avalanche hazard when snow-covered

waysIn.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — summer scramble
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, once the couloir has melted to talus
waysIn.notes: Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) to the Esmeralda Basin road-end parking at about 4,243 ft. A quarter mile of old mining road leads to a fork; take the right branch for Longs Pass. The trail climbs an open, south-facing hillside with essentially no shade — in July and August this is a pre-dawn start, not a preference. Longs Pass sits around 6,200-6,250 ft, roughly 2,000 ft above the car in about two miles, and it is the single most useful place on the whole approach. From the pass, drop the steep loose scree on the north side, losing 1,200-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft. Cross the creek — there is a summer log crossing, and in high melt it is worth walking to find it rather than wading — then follow the Ingalls Creek Trail upvalley (west) a short way to the meadow and camps below the couloir's outlet. Good camps sit on the valley floor more or less straight south of where the couloir comes down, with a few more near the footlog. From camp a climbers' path threads the meadow to the toe of the couloir. This is also the standard descent for the North Ridge, West Ridge and most of the rest of Stuart, so expect to share it.
hazards: Sun-exposed hillside to Longs Pass with no water and no shade
Ingalls Creek can run high in early-season melt; find the summer log rather than fording blind
The couloir is loose top to bottom — sand, scree and unstable blocks; serious rockfall risk from parties above
Upper couloir braids into a maze of use-paths and cairns; genuinely confusing in cloud or at dawn/dusk
The 8,800 ft snowfield must be passed on the climber's left

waysIn.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — spring snow climb
waysIn.season: May-Jun as a snow route; road access is the limiting factor earlier
waysIn.notes:
The same line, in a completely different medium. With the couloir snow-filled it is a straightforward steep snow climb rather than a scree grind, and many parties prefer it this way — but it demands axe and crampons, an early start, and a hard turnaround, because the whole thing faces south and softens fast.

FR 9737 is a gravel road that is not maintained through winter and is generally not clear until late June in a heavy year, so a genuinely early-season attempt means adding road miles on foot or ski. Check the road before committing.

The Longs Pass hillside carries avalanche exposure in winter and spring conditions, and the north-side drop to Ingalls Creek holds snow that can be firm and icy at dawn and slushy by mid-morning.
hazards: FR 9737 unmaintained in winter/spring — verify access before driving out
Avalanche exposure on the Longs Pass hillside and in the couloir itself
South-facing: wet-slide and rockfall risk build through the day, so an early turnaround is not optional
Firm/icy snow at dawn on the north side of Longs Pass
Uncontrolled glissade on descent
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late spring, while the couloir is still filled with snow and gives a faster, steeper snow climb than the summer scree; needs axe and crampons and an early start before it softens.

name: Girth Pillar
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (Trail #1599, ~3,400') off Icicle Creek Rd/FS-7601, follow the trail up Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake junction (~4,600') and stay right for Stuart Lake. About a mile farther, leave the trail where it turns uphill for Stuart Lake: cross Mountaineer Creek on logs, follow the climbers' path up the valley bottom, and climb steepening talus and heather benches directly toward the basin beneath the Ice Cliff Glacier on Stuart's northeast face (moraine camps around 6,800-7,000'). This off-trail stretch is loose and exposed to rockfall — expect real route-finding, especially in the dark on an alpine start. From camp, rope up and climb the Ice Cliff Glacier itself: this is the route's main objective hazard, with significant icefall, spindrift, and crevasse danger — parties typically stay left to dodge falling ice and swing wide right to avoid the glacier's largest crevasses. At the top of the glacier is the 'ice cliff' step itself, anywhere from 10 to 100+ feet of 50-70° snow/ice (easier and shorter early season, steeper and more likely bare ice as the season progresses). Above the step, four moderate pitches of rock lead to the base of the Girth Pillar proper (~8,200-8,400'). There is no water source above the moraine camp — carry what you need for the climb, or plan to melt snow/ice.
descent: The route tops out on easier ground above the pillar, leading to the false summit above the Ice Cliff Glacier and on to Stuart's true summit. There is no reasonable way to reverse the route — down-climbing or rappelling back through the Ice Cliff Glacier's icefall and crevasse hazard is considerably more dangerous than finishing over the top, so continuing to the summit is effectively mandatory. From the true summit, retrace toward the false summit and descend the Sherpa Glacier, entered just east of where the Ice Cliff Glacier couloir tops out near 8,200 ft, back to the moraine camp; later in the season, once the Sherpa has melted out, parties go around Sherpa Peak to Sherpa Pass instead. Then walk out the Mountaineer Creek climbers' trail to the Stuart Lake trailhead, the same one used for the approach, so no car shuttle is needed. The glacier descent is technical, especially in the dark, so keep the axe, crampons and crevasse kit for it. If a party needs to bail from partway up the pillar itself, the crack pitches would need to be rappelled on natural gear anchors (no fixed hardware is reported on the pillar) — a real possibility to plan for given the route's commitment, but not part of the standard descent.
hazards: Large loose blocks reported on the P3 (5.10+) pitch — test holds carefully.
Icefall/crevasse hazard shared with the Ice Cliff Glacier approach beneath the pillar.

waysIn.name: Ice Cliff Glacier to the top of the ice, then four easy pitches to the pillar
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. The ice cliff step is shorter and more amenable early and gets steeper and barer as the season runs on, so the rock and the ice want opposite conditions
waysIn.notes:
The approach is the Ice Cliff Glacier's approach, and everything said about that line applies here: from the Stuart Lake trailhead follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake junction, leave it where it turns uphill for Stuart Lake, cross Mountaineer Creek and follow the climbers' path in the valley bottom to the hanging basin under the glaciers. Moraine camps sit around 6,800-7,000 ft; the flat basin below at about 5,400 ft is the more common bivy.

From camp the route ropes up and climbs the Ice Cliff Glacier itself. That glacier is the objective hazard of the day, not the pillar: icefall, spindrift and crevasses. Parties keep left to stay out from under the falling ice and swing wide right around the biggest crevasses.

At the top of the glacier is the ice cliff step, anywhere from ten to well over a hundred feet of 50-70 degree snow and ice.

There is no water above the moraine — carry it or melt.
hazards: Icefall and serac collapse on the Ice Cliff Glacier — the route's principal danger
Crevasses and spindrift on the glacier
A steep ice cliff step whose height and hardness vary through the season
Large loose blocks near the top of the pillar
No retreat: reversing the route through the icefall is more dangerous than continuing over the summit
No water above the moraine camp

name: Ice Cliff Glacier
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of Eightmile Road/FR 7601 off Icicle Road/FR 7600), follow the main trail toward Stuart Lake, staying right at the fork, then leave the trail before the final switchbacks, cross the creek, and follow a climbers' path up the Mountaineer Creek valley to campsites around 5,400 ft beneath the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers.
descent: Descend via the Sherpa Glacier, starting near the false summit (~8,200 ft), back down into the basin below the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers, then retrace the approach to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. Do not down-climb the ice route.
hazards: Icefall from the hanging ice cliff itself — trip reports document large chunks breaking off and shattering on the route below climbers; this is the route's signature objective hazard.
Crevasses on the lower Ice Cliff Glacier, worsening in late season and as the glacier continues to recede.
A cornice can guard the top of the couloir exit in some years, adding a technical crux beyond the ice pitch.

waysIn.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Mountaineer Creek valley to the 5,400 ft basin
waysIn.season: Roughly Apr-Jun; the ice cliff and the couloir exit get harder and more broken as the season runs on
waysIn.notes: Start at the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, about 3,400 ft. Follow the main trail to the first fork, roughly two and a half to three miles in near 4,600 ft, and stay right for Stuart Lake. Left is Colchuck Lake, a different basin on the other side of the ridge. About a mile to a mile and a half past that junction, the Stuart Lake trail turns uphill and swings right, away from the water, and begins switchbacking. That turn is your cue. Leave the trail there and stay flat in the valley bottom with Mountaineer Creek. The test is simple and works in poor visibility: if you are gaining elevation on switchbacks you are walking to Stuart Lake and you have missed it. Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs. There is no single canonical log and parties describe several sporty crossings that shift with the snowpack; early season, snowbanks make dropping onto a log awkward. On the far side, pick up the climbers' path along the creek. It is unmaintained, full of blowdown and re-routes, and the cairns are not to be trusted: they invite you up and right into a boulder slope around 4,675 ft. Two parties independently say stay low beside the creek instead, with the creek on your left — the path is unpleasant but the better line. Some parties do use the boulder field deliberately to avoid the creek crossings, so treat it as a genuine choice rather than a mistake. After about a mile and a half the valley steepens. Turn right and west and climb talus and forest into a hanging flat basin at about 5,400 ft, under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers. That right-turn-and-climb out of a steepening valley into flat ground is the arrival cue for the bivy.
hazards: Serac fall from the hanging ice cliff you traverse beneath — a party watched a large piece break away and shatter on the ledge below them
Rockfall and avalanche in the couloir
Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the lower glacier
A cornice at the couloir exit, which becomes the crux when large
An unmaintained climbers' trail with blowdown and misleading cairns
Sporty log crossings of Mountaineer Creek, worse under early-season snow

waysIn.name: Early-season approach with the Eightmile road gated
waysIn.season: Spring, roughly Apr-May, when the route is in as snow and ice
waysIn.notes:
When Eightmile Road is snowed or gated below the trailhead, add roughly two and a half miles of road before the trail proper. Parties walk that stretch and then put skis on, skinning the Stuart Lake trail, before continuing on foot.

This is a genuinely different day rather than a longer walk: the valley is snow-covered, the log crossings may be buried or may be harder to reach off a snowbank, and the boulder-field-versus-creek question largely disappears under snow. Postholing on the cross-country section is the common complaint.

No reliable published trailhead-to-bivy time exists for either version, so plan from your own pace rather than from a number.
hazards: Avalanche on the approach slopes and in the couloir
Buried or unreachable log crossings
Deep postholing once off skis
Extra road mileage each way when the gate is down
waysIn.whyThisWay: Early spring, when snow or a gate closes Eightmile Road short of the trailhead and the party must add road miles on foot or skis before the usual trail.

name: North Ridge (Complete)
approach: Primary approach is from the north via the Stuart Lake Trailhead (reached via Icicle Creek Road and FR 7601 out of Leavenworth). From the trailhead, follow the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trail as it rolls along Mountaineer Creek through forest; at the signed junction roughly 2 miles in, stay right on the Stuart Lake Trail (the Colchuck Lake Trail is the left fork). Continue up the Mountaineer Creek valley on the Stuart Lake Trail, then leave the maintained trail before reaching Stuart Lake itself, cross Mountaineer Creek, and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. After roughly 2 more miles of streamside travel, climb a steep, loose talus/boulder slope to gain the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier — this valley has good bivy sites and is a common overnight stop. From the valley, angle directly up to the toe of the North Ridge, keeping the Ice Cliff Glacier on your left; the notch/base of the upper ridge sits around 8,200 ft, where a snow-filled gully (often climbed on 4th-class rock at its edge) gains the crest. All-in this is roughly 6-6.5 miles and 3,300+ ft of gain, about 4-5 hours to the base of the climbing. A well-known alternative is the southern approach via the Esmeralda/Teanaway trailhead over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, gaining the ridge from that side (~9 miles, ~4,800 ft gain, ~8 hours) — longer and higher-gain on the way in, but it sets up a much shorter car-to-car loop for parties planning to descend the Cascadian Couloir, since that descent drops back toward Ingalls Creek. Water is available at Mountaineer Creek and its south fork on the north approach, and at Ingalls Creek/seasonal snow patches near the 8,200 ft notch bivy on the south approach; above the notch there is no reliable water. Route-finding through the boulder/talus slope below Sherpa Glacier and the creek crossing (higher and faster in early season) are the main approach-specific hazards.
descent: Nearly all parties descend via the Cascadian Couloir on the mountain's south side — this is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required (0 rappels) under normal summer conditions. From the true summit, downclimb steep snow or scree, keeping right through sparse trees to drop into the head of the Cascadian Couloir, then follow the couloir down its full length (loose sand, scree, and rockfall-prone rock the entire way; an ice axe, and often crampons, are recommended into mid-summer for a lingering snow tongue) to the valley floor near Ingalls Creek, roughly 4,000 ft below the summit. The upper couloir splits into a confusing maze of climbers' paths and cairns — keep to the established talus path on the climber's left side around the 8,800 ft permanent snowfield; parties who drift onto the right side have run into old rappel-station remnants and much harder downclimbing. Because the North Ridge is climbed from the north (Stuart Lake/Mountaineer Creek side) while the Cascadian Couloir exits to the south (Ingalls Creek/Teanaway side), most parties face a long, tiring hike back around the mountain to a north-side vehicle — either via Longs Pass and a car shuttle, or a full trail loop back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead; parties using the southern (Esmeralda/Longs Pass) approach avoid this by parking on that side to begin with. Note: some parties opt for a short, optional ~75 ft rappel off the right side of the ridge below the Great Gendarme (using an established, well-traveled sling/fixed anchor, not bolted) to bypass the crux 5.9 pitches during the ascent — this is a mid-route bypass rappel, not part of the standard descent, and is not counted in the rappel total below. A single 60m rope doubled (or a single-strand lower) is sufficient for it.
hazards: Exposed, sometimes loose rock along the long ridge crest, especially on the traverse pitches around the Gendarme.
Afternoon thunderstorms are a real risk on a route this long and exposed — an early start and a weather eye are essential.
The Cascadian Couloir descent carries significant rockfall hazard; many parties are more tired and less careful on the way down.

waysIn.name: North side — Stuart Lake TH via Mountaineer Creek
waysIn.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.
hazards: Mountaineer Creek and its south fork run high and fast in early-season melt
Loose talus and boulder slope below the Sherpa Glacier basin, rockfall onto parties below
Serac and icefall exposure if you drift east under the Ice Cliff Glacier
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch once its snow patch is gone
