Descent exits on the opposite side of the range, so a shuttle or long walk-around is needed
Exposed, sometimes loose rock along the ridge crest and around the Gendarme
Afternoon thunderstorms; rockfall on the Cascadian Couloir descent

waysIn.name: South side — Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and Goat Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, once the traverse under the Stuart Glacier has melted or consolidated
waysIn.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.
hazards: Snow slopes on the Goat Pass traverse reported near 40 degrees; conditions change through summer
About 2,000 ft of descent on the way in that must be regained on the way out
Long day with no bail-out once past Goat Pass; approach consistently underestimated
Traverse under the Stuart Glacier with route-finding rather than tread
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch
Exposed, sometimes loose rock along the ridge crest and around the Gendarme
Afternoon thunderstorms; rockfall on the Cascadian Couloir descent
waysIn.whyThisWay: When avoiding the car shuttle: the usual Cascadian Couloir descent lands on this side, so the party walks out to its own car, at the cost of a longer, higher approach.

name: Stuart Glacier Couloir
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of Eightmile Road/FR 7601, off Icicle Road/FR 7600), follow the Mountaineer Creek climbers' path past the Colchuck Lake turnoff toward the basins below the north side of the mountain, then work up into the Stuart Glacier basin beneath the col shared with the West Ridge.
descent: The couloir exits at or near the notch on the West Ridge, with a little more low fifth-class ridge to the summit. From the top, the usual way down is south by the Cascadian Couloir: cross the Class 2-3 ground between the true and false summits (steep, often corniced snow early in the season), drop into the couloir and follow it down loose scree and talus to Ingalls Creek, then regain Longs Pass and walk out to the Esmeralda trailhead. Parties camped in the basin below the north side often prefer the Sherpa Glacier instead, which is the better early-season way back to camp. Carry an ice axe for the Cascadian, and keep clear of other parties, because the couloir sheds rock.
hazards: narrow couloir funnels rockfall
bergschrund at base
steep firm snow/ice

waysIn.name: Mountaineer Creek to the basin, then west onto the Stuart Glacier
waysIn.season: Best while the couloir holds continuous snow and the steps take ice, roughly late spring into early summer; later the steps go rocky and the climbing turns mixed
waysIn.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the trail about three miles to the Colchuck Lake turnoff and continue past it for roughly another mile. Where the Stuart Lake trail switchbacks up and to the right, veer left to stay in the main valley — the same leaving point every north-side route on this mountain uses.

Follow the valley about a mile and a half to where it steepens, then turn right and work up the steep slope into the small hanging valley above, the flat basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers at roughly 5,400 ft. Standard camp is here.

From the basin the route continues west, round the far side of the North Ridge, onto the Stuart Glacier. Entry to the couloir is at about 7,800 ft.

The couloir itself runs 40-50 degree snow, narrows to a short steep step whose character depends entirely on the season, then a second shorter step, then opens into a wider snowfield leading to a notch in the West Ridge. Six pitches of mixed ground follow from that notch to the summit.
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier below the couloir
Rockfall and wet-snow avalanche in the couloir as the day warms
Narrow couloir funnels rockfall; bergschrund at the base
Steep steps that turn to bare ice or dry-tooling ground later in the season
Six pitches of mixed climbing above the notch, on the far side of the mountain from camp
Unmarked, often snow-covered off-trail turn out of the Mountaineer Creek valley

waysIn.name: Esmeralda, Ingalls Lake and Stuart Pass to Goat Pass
waysIn.notes: From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead, hike over Ingalls Pass to Ingalls Lake, then traverse toward Stuart Pass. Near 7,000 ft cross the scree gully north to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft, where there is plenty of bivy ground. From the pass descend a short way onto the Stuart Glacier and traverse under the North Ridge to the couloir; the glacier passes above some large crevasses.
hazards: Traverse on the Stuart Glacier passes above some large crevasses
Snow crossings under the glacier well into summer; the Goat Pass camp is dry late in the season
Narrow couloir funnels rockfall; bergschrund at the base
Rockfall and wet-snow avalanche in the couloir as the day warms
Steep firm snow and ice, turning to mixed dry-tooling in early season
Rockfall on the West Ridge finish
waysIn.whyThisWay: When approaching from the south side, over Ingalls and Stuart Passes to Goat Pass, with a high bivy and a short drop onto the glacier; the northern Mountaineer Creek route is longer.

name: West Ridge
approach: Start at the Esmeralda Trailhead (end of North Fork Teanaway Road, ~4,243 ft) and follow the Ingalls Way Trail. At about 0.3 mile, stay right onto Ingalls Way where it leaves the Esmeralda Basin Trail; at about 1.7 miles (5,440 ft), turn right at the Longs Pass junction rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin, and switchback up open slopes to Longs Pass (roughly 3 mi, ~2,100 ft gain from the trailhead, cresting around 6,400 ft) — the pass gives the first clear look at Stuart's west aspect. From the pass, descend steep, sometimes dusty/scree-y trail on the north side, losing about 1,300 ft in a mile, to reach Ingalls Creek in the timber below. Cross the creek (a straightforward rock-hop or wade in normal summer flow, the last reliable water source before the ridge) and pick up the climber's path heading west, up-valley, toward Stuart Pass. Well short of the pass itself (roughly 6,200–6,400 ft), leave the trail and traverse climber's-left (north) across open talus and heather benches toward the base of the West Ridge — this cross-country traverse is where parties most commonly go astray, since there is no maintained tread and several minor gullies look similar; aim for the obvious deep gully (the middle of three parallel gullies) marked by a large, house-sized boulder at its base. An alternate, longer northern approach via the Stuart Lake Trailhead and Stuart Pass exists but adds significant mileage and is not the standard line. Plan on 3.5–5 hours car-to-base depending on route-finding and snow conditions; some parties camp near Ingalls Lake or in the upper Ingalls Creek basin to break the day up. Hazards: the Longs Pass descent and creek-crossing slopes hold snow into early summer and can be icy at dawn; the final talus traverse to the ridge is loose and exposed to rockfall from parties above; there is no water beyond the Ingalls Creek crossing, so tank up there for the long day ahead. Getting past Long John Tower and the exposed West Ridge Notch traverse are the route's main route-finding dilemmas; high on the route, below the summit, a short dihedral with a fixed piton (5.4) or a layback further along the ledge (5.6) leads to easier fifth-class climbing to the top.
descent: Descend via the Cascadian Couloir, the standard walk-off for the entire Stuart massif — this is a scramble descent, not a rappel route, under normal (dry to firm-snow) conditions. From the summit, reverse the short 3rd/2nd-class scramble east along the summit ridge to the false summit (~9,200 ft), then drop into the broken rock and scree above the top of the couloir. Stay climber's-right through sparse trees and rock bands near the top to find the true couloir entrance rather than dropping into parallel gullies to the left, which cliff out. From there it's a sustained, direct descent of loose scree/talus (snow early season) losing about 4,000 ft to the floor of the Ingalls Creek valley — many parties glissade or boot-ski the upper snowfield when it's in, which is markedly faster and easier on the knees than the bare-scree version later in summer. Watch for sun cups and inconsistent snow texture on the upper couloir, and expect significant rockfall exposure funneled by the gully, especially with other parties above or below. At the bottom, pick up a climber's path through meadows to the Ingalls Creek Trail near the Longs Pass turnoff, then reverse the approach (back over Longs Pass) to the Esmeralda Trailhead. No rappels are required on this descent in normal conditions; a fixed/natural rock anchor has been reported near the false summit that some parties use to rappel the initial short, steep, icy step off the summit ridge in early-season or verglassed conditions, but this is a discretionary variation, not a standard part of the descent, and the anchor is not maintained or guaranteed. Total summit-to-trailhead time is commonly 3–5 hours for a fit party in good conditions. In August the Cascadian descent is long and loose; watch for the trail turn-off near 6,000 ft that leads out to the creek and trailhead, as missing it costs a lot of effort.
hazards: Route-finding on a long ridge with several towers and notches
Loose rock in places; exposure on the crest
Long approach and descent make for a big day
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge

waysIn.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass to upper Ingalls Creek
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep for dry rock; snow lingers on the Longs Pass north side into early summer
waysIn.notes:
From the Esmeralda trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail (it leaves the Esmeralda Basin Trail at about 0.3 mile) and, at the junction about 1.7 miles from the car, near 5,440 ft, turn right for Longs Pass rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin. Switchback up open slopes to the pass, which gives the first clear view of Stuart's west side.

Descend the steep dusty north side of the pass, losing about 1,300 ft in a mile, and cross Ingalls Creek in the timber below. In normal summer flow this is a rock-hop; it is also the last reliable water before the ridge, so fill up.

Pick up the climbers' path heading west up the valley toward Stuart Pass. You leave it well short of Stuart Pass, in the upper meadows at roughly 6,200-6,400 ft, and traverse climber's-left (north) across talus and heather benches to the foot of the ridge. There is no tread on this traverse and it is the part of the day people get wrong.

Some parties break the approach by camping near Ingalls Lake or in the upper Ingalls Creek basin.
hazards: No maintained tread on the talus/heather traverse from the Stuart Pass trail to the ridge — several minor gullies look alike
Steep loose descent off the north side of Longs Pass; icy at dawn in early summer
Loose talus below the ridge with rockfall exposure from parties above
No water past the Ingalls Creek crossing
Descent is the Cascadian Couloir, and 'not staying right' near the top of it is a documented route-finding error

name: Mount Teneriffe Trail (Standard Route)
approach: From I-90 take Exit 31 into North Bend and continue on North Bend Way; turn left (north) on SE Mount Si Road. Continue about 2.9 miles, past the Little Si and Mount Si trailheads, to the paved, ~70-car Mount Teneriffe Trailhead lot (Discover Pass required). From the lot, a half-mile access path switchbacks up through second-growth forest to an old logging-road grade, which climbs gently for about 1.5 miles through young forest and meadow, passing the signed spur to Teneriffe Falls at about 0.9 mile. Beyond the road grade the trail narrows and climbs via switchbacks (with a Middle Fork Snoqualmie viewpoint) for another ~2.7 miles, then continues about 2.3 more miles, dipping briefly to Rachor Pass (~4,200 ft saddle) before the final short, rocky summit scramble. The trailhead gate was reported locked at about 8 pm and unlocked around 7 am in May and August, so budget the descent to beat it.
descent: From the summit, downclimb the same short rocky scramble to Rachor Pass, then follow the Mount Teneriffe Trail back down through the switchbacks past the Teneriffe Falls junction to the trailhead, retracing the ascent for roughly 3,800 ft of loss over 6.5 miles. Parties who ascended via the Kamikaze Trail can instead continue down this standard trail through Rachor Pass to close a ~10-mile loop, avoiding the steep, often wet Kamikaze boot track on the way down.
hazards: Seasonal snow lingers on the upper mountain and ridge crest into June, creating steep, icy sections on an otherwise Class 1-2 trail.
No reliable water sources beyond Teneriffe Falls; carry sufficient water for the full round trip.
The trailhead gate closes seasonally (roughly an hour before dusk); vehicles left past closing risk being locked in.

waysIn.name: Mount Teneriffe Trail from the paved trailhead
waysIn.season: March to November, best from June to October. Snow lingers on the upper mountain and ridge crest into June and makes an otherwise easy trail steep and icy.
waysIn.notes: From the freeway exit into North Bend, continue through town and turn north onto the road running below the peaks. Carry on 2.9 miles, past the Little Si and Mount Si trailheads, to the paved seventy-car lot — this is the Teneriffe trailhead, not the Si one, and the two are easy to confuse. A short access path switchbacks up to an old logging-road grade, which climbs gently for a mile and a half through young forest and meadow. The trailhead gate closes seasonally about an hour before dusk; vehicles left past closing risk being locked in.
hazards: Seasonal snow on the upper mountain and ridge crest into June, creating steep icy sections on otherwise easy trail
No reliable water beyond the falls — carry what you need for the round trip
The trailhead gate closes seasonally about an hour before dusk

name: North Face / North Buttress
approach: From the Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead (elev. ~600 ft, reached via the unpaved Goodell Creek Road that turns north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground), follow the old abandoned roadbed/boot path northeast along Goodell Creek for roughly 4 to 4.5 miles — gentle grade, easy walking — to a stone-cairn/arrow junction near 1,700 ft marking the start of the climbers' path up toward Terror Basin. Do not continue straight past the cairn; that fainter track follows Terror Creek toward Crescent Creek Basin and is a separate (and notoriously brushier) approach. Instead take the hard right and start up the steep, well-beaten Terror Basin boot path, which climbs directly and relentlessly through old-growth forest — roughly 3,000+ ft of gain in about 1.5 miles — before breaking out above treeline around 5,000–5,200 ft. Above the trees, a rising traverse across heather benches, slabs, and (early-season) snowfields leads to a broad saddle near 6,200 ft; the standard high camp is in a gravelly, wildflower basin about 400 ft below and beyond the saddle, around 5,800 ft, fed by several small streams (reliable water). From this Terror Basin camp, parties continue over the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin and camp again there before the climb. Hazards: the boot path itself is the crux of the approach — steep, root-and-dirt, unrelentingly brushy in places, and physically punishing (widely regarded as one of the harder approaches in the Pickets); expect loose rock and route-finding on the upper slabs approaching the saddle; if the alternate Terror Creek/Crescent Creek Basin line is used, a creek ford or logjam crossing of Terror Creek is required. Most parties treat this as a two-day approach with a high camp rather than a car-to-base push. The technical start of the North Face is reached from the Crescent Creek Basin camp by crossing the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descending the Mustard Glacier into McMillan Cirque to the foot of Terror's wall, a 2-3 hour trip even for fast parties. By mid-to-late summer the Mustard Glacier below the face is heavily crevassed with mostly unbridged, broken ice; carry glacier travel gear even though it's a small glacier.
descent: The North Face and any north-side buttress lines are steep and complex enough that essentially no one reverses them — virtually all parties, regardless of which route they climbed, descend via the West Ridge. From the summit, downclimb/scramble the West Ridge crest westward toward the low notch between Terror and The Rake, where a large chockstone marks the top of the descent gully system. From there, work down a narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully back into Crescent Creek Basin. The exact count varies with snow coverage and route-finding — figure roughly 3–5 rappels total: commonly one or two shorter raps off slung horns/chockstones or fixed pitons-and-a-nut near the ridge crest, followed by two or three more rappels down the gully itself with down-climbing in between. A single 50–60m rope is sufficient for every station reported; anchors are a mix of pre-existing fixed slings/rap rings and natural chockstone/horn anchors that may need backing up with your own gear. The gully is narrow with little shelter from rockfall, frequently has an undercut, melted-out snow moat by mid-to-late season, and the final ~100 ft is loose and marginal — expect stuck ropes in the confined terrain and manage rope ends carefully. Once down in Crescent Creek Basin, parties either regain the Barrier saddle to return to a Terror Basin camp, or exit directly via the Crescent Creek Basin/Terror Creek climbers' path, which follows the Barrier crest south before dropping to rejoin the Goodell Creek Trail for the hike out.
hazards: Heavily crevassed Mustard Glacier ice on the way to the base, mostly unbridged by late summer
Extreme remoteness — a multi-day, off-trail carry-over just to reach the base
Loose rock in the approach gullies and on both the Cooper line and Stoddard Buttress
Complex descent, typically down the opposite (south) side of the mountain
Essentially no cell coverage; among the most rescue-difficult terrain in North Cascades NP

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Basin boot path, then over the Barrier to Crescent Creek Basin and the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col to the foot of the wall
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead at about 600 ft, reached via the unpaved Goodell Creek Road that turns north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground, follow the old abandoned roadbed and boot path northeast along Goodell Creek for roughly 4-4.5 miles of gentle grade to a stone-cairn and arrow junction near 1,700 ft.

Do not continue straight past the cairn. That fainter track follows Terror Creek toward Crescent Creek Basin and is a separate, notoriously brushier approach. Instead take the hard right and start up the steep, well-beaten Terror Basin boot path, which climbs directly through old-growth forest, roughly 3,000-plus ft of gain in about 1.5 miles, before breaking out above treeline around 5,000-5,200 ft.

Above the trees a rising traverse across heather benches, slabs and early-season snowfields leads to a broad saddle near 6,200 ft; the standard high camp is in a gravelly, wildflower basin about 400 ft below and beyond the saddle, around 5,800 ft, fed by several small streams.
hazards: Committing to the wrong rib on a 2,000 ft face with limited options to reverse
A heavily crevassed, mostly unbridged Mustard Glacier below the face by mid-season
Steep, extremely loose rock near the top; a fatal-consequence rockfall accident on this buttress involved a block that had appeared solid
A narrow, rockfall-prone descent gully with an undercut melted-out moat by mid to late season
Stuck ropes in the confined descent gully, and a loose, marginal final 100 ft
Retreat from high on the route is genuinely difficult

name: East Ridge
approach: From the Goodell Creek trailhead off SR-20 near Newhalem, follow the old roadbed and Terror Basin climbers' path (~4 miles, then a steep, cairned side trail) to the 5,800' Terror Basin camp, then continue over the roughly 6,400' Chopping Block col into Crescent Creek Basin. The saddle between Terror and Degenhardt is reached from the basin via slabs and talus on its east side.
descent: Descend the West Ridge rather than reversing the East Ridge. From the summit, retrace the Class 3-4 ground and scramble ridge down to the low notch between Terror and The Rake, then go down the gully on the far side into Crescent Creek Basin. The gully is deep, narrow and loose, so expect rockfall and, in early season, snow or ice; it is descended with several rappels, including off a large chockstone, and downclimbing between them. The lower ridge has established anchors about 25 m apart, which suit short rappels or a belayed downclimb. Once in the basin, walk back to the Crescent Creek camp.
hazards: Notoriously loose, choss-prone rock along the ridge
Rarely traveled — limited fixed anchors/current beta
Exposed slab traverse to/from the Degenhardt–Terror saddle

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek and Terror Basin, over the Chopping Block col into Crescent Creek Basin, then slabs and talus on the east side to the Terror-Degenhardt saddle
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead off SR-20 near Newhalem, follow the old roadbed and Terror Basin climbers' path, about 4 miles then a steep cairned side trail, to the 5,800 ft Terror Basin camp, then continue over the roughly 6,400 ft Chopping Block col into Crescent Creek Basin.
hazards: A descent by a different route than the one climbed, off a large chockstone in a loose gully
The Chopping Block col and Crescent Creek Basin traverse before any climbing
Loose rock throughout, in a range where that is the defining characteristic
The full Goodell Creek approach with roughly 6,000 ft of gain to camp

name: West Ridge
approach: From Goodell Creek trailhead, follow the old roadbed ~4.5 miles, cross Terror Creek, and climb a steep climber's track (pink flagging, moss-covered cliffs) to reach Crescent Creek Basin; total approach elevation gain to basecamp is nearly 6,000 ft.
descent: Downclimb the summit tower or rappel a short section back to the notch, using existing sling anchors there, then descend the steep choss gully back toward Crescent Creek Basin with two or three rappels and downclimbing between them — take care with loose rock and, in early season, snow/ice in the gully.
hazards: Pervasive loose rock on both the approach gully and ridge
Snow/ice in the gully in early season
Remote location with no quick rescue option

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek, the Terror Creek crossing and the flagged climber's track into Crescent Creek Basin, then the west gully to the chockstone notch
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead, follow the old roadbed about 4.5 miles, cross Terror Creek, and climb a steep climber's track marked with pink flagging past moss-covered cliffs to reach Crescent Creek Basin. Total approach gain to basecamp is nearly 6,000 ft.

This is the standard descent route for every north-side line on the peak, so it sees traffic in both directions and its features are described mostly from above.
hazards: A narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully with little shelter
An undercut, melted-out snow moat in the gully by mid to late season
A loose and marginal final 100 ft of the gully
Stuck ropes in the confined terrain
Dropping into Crescent Creek Basin from the wrong notch north of the Chopping Block
Early-season snow and ice in the choss gully

name: West Ridge
approach: Park at the PCT North (Commonwealth Basin) Trailhead lot just off the frontage road at Exit 52, Snoqualmie Pass (~3,000 ft) — cross under I-90, take the first right, and the lot is on the right. From the trailhead, follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; it climbs steadily through timber via long switchbacks for roughly 5.5–6 miles to the Kendall Katwalk (~5,400 ft), a narrow, exposed ledge blasted directly into a granite cliff on the ridge north of Kendall Peak — solid underfoot but very exposed, use caution if icy or in high wind. Continue north on the PCT about a mile past the Katwalk, dropping slightly, to Ridge Lake (~5,260 ft), the last reliable water source and a common camp/rest stop (roughly 2–2.5 hrs / ~7 mi in from the car). About 0.4–0.5 mile past Ridge Lake, watch for an unsigned but obvious climbers' boot path branching left (west) off the PCT; it climbs a steep ~200 ft to Bumblebee Pass (~5,400 ft), a small saddle above Alaska Lake. The path is loose and eroded in spots on both the up and down sides — take care with footing. Drop off the far side of the pass into Bumblebee Basin (scattered camps, seasonal water), then contour/ascend northwest across talus and scree (worse-looking than it climbs) toward the lowest notch on Thomson's west ridgeline (~5,960 ft). Short sections of 4th-class scrambling around a set of gendarmes lead to the notch at the base of the route, where the first pitch starts just left (north) of the crest. Total trailhead-to-base distance is about 8–8.5 miles with roughly 2,900–3,000 ft of gain, typically 4–5 hours for a fit party; most groups do the climb car-to-car in one long day, though the basin makes a fine camp for a two-day trip.
descent: From the true summit, the standard descent follows the East Ridge back toward Bumblebee Pass rather than reversing the West Ridge climb. Walk/scramble off the east end of the summit block on a faint climbers' path to a notch where several parties over the years have left fixed tree anchors (webbing and rap rings, not bolts) at three points along the ridge's steeper steps — roughly around 6,200 ft and lower. Descent style varies by party and conditions: some downclimb the entire East Ridge unroped (sustained, exposed class 3–4 with a couple of low-5th moves), while most rope up for at least one section. A common approach is a single double-rope rappel (60m rope, doubled) off the initial tree anchor to bypass the steepest, most exposed step, then class 3 scrambling the rest of the way down; other parties describe using two to three shorter rappels off successive tree stations (doubled 8mm/thin rope, ~30m per rap) where the rock is loose or holds are wet, downclimbing the easier sections between them. Inspect any tat/rap rings before weighting them and back them up or replace old webbing if in doubt — these are climber-maintained natural anchors, not resupplied by any agency. Once off the ridge's technical ground, descend talus back into Bumblebee Basin, regain the steep boot path up and over Bumblebee Pass, drop back to the PCT near Ridge Lake, and retrace the Kendall Katwalk and switchbacks south to the PCT North Trailhead.
hazards: Loose rock
Exposure
Route-finding on approach and ridge
Afternoon thunderstorms
Lingering early-season snow on the approach

waysIn.name: PCT to Bumblebee Pass, into the basin, then the lowest notch on the west ridge
waysIn.season: July to September
waysIn.notes:
Park at the PCT North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass, about 3,000 ft: cross under I-90, take the first right, lot on the right. Follow the PCT northbound through timber on long switchbacks for roughly 5.5 to 6 miles to the Kendall Katwalk at about 5,400 ft, a narrow ledge blasted into a granite cliff on the ridge north of Kendall Peak — solid underfoot, very exposed, and worth care if icy or windy.

Continue north about a mile past the Katwalk, dropping slightly, to Ridge Lake at about 5,260 ft, the last reliable water and a common camp; roughly two to two and a half hours and about seven miles from the car.

About 0.4 to 0.5 mile past Ridge Lake, watch for an unsigned but obvious climbers' boot path branching left (west) off the PCT. It climbs a steep 200 ft to Bumblebee Pass at about 5,400 ft, above Alaska Lake. Drop off the far side into Bumblebee Basin, then contour and climb northwest across talus and scree toward the ridge.

About 8 to 8.5 miles and 2,900 to 3,000 ft to the base, typically four to five hours for a fit party.
hazards: The Kendall Katwalk, exposed and dangerous when icy or windy
Loose and eroded tread on both sides of the Bumblebee Pass boot path
Talus and scree in the basin below the ridge
A descent by the East Ridge, meaning a route-finding descent on unfamiliar ground at the end of a long day
A long day: many parties climb it car to car

name: South Ridge
approach: Start at the Boston Basin Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road/FR-15). The unmaintained but well-beaten climbers' trail switchbacks steeply up through forest and traverses west, crossing a couple of small creeks (reliable water), to reach the meadows of Boston Basin in roughly 1.5-3.5 hours depending on pace and pack weight. Established low camps sit around 5,300 ft on the basin's tundra benches; from there, continue climbing skier's-right of Boston Creek (a good water source until it's dry/frozen) up open slabs and tundra to the upper high camp near 6,400-6,600 ft, below Sharkfin Tower and Forbidden Peak's south spur. From high camp, do a rising traverse northwest at roughly the 6,200 ft contour, staying beneath Forbidden's south spur, cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, and continue toward the toe of the Taboo Glacier. Gain the glacier on its left (climber's left) side and follow it up until a deep gully/couloir breaks through the rock band on the left; a bergschrund or moat typically has to be negotiated here and has been the site of a fatal accident, so treat the crossing seriously, especially early season when it's snow-bridged or late season when it's wide open. Scramble up the gully (class 3-4, loose in spots — helmet recommended) to the South Ridge notch/South Col. Expect firm snow or glacier ice on the approach slopes early in the season (crampons/axe useful) and a short glacier crossing that warrants basic crevasse-rescue readiness even though it is generally low-angle and short.
descent: Three options exist, and the choice depends on party speed and whether you're continuing to Forbidden Peak. (1) Reverse the South Ridge: downclimb interspersed with numerous short, traversing rappels off fixed slings/anchors that are 'in abundance' along the ridge — a single rope is generally sufficient for these short raps, but carry extra webbing/cord to back up or replace tat, since stations are alpine-style (slung horns, chockstones, occasional old fixed gear) rather than bolted. This option is slower but avoids the moat problems of the SE Face line. (2) Descend the Southeast Face: downclimb from the summit area to the top rappel station, then make 5-6 double-rope (60m) rappels down the SE Face gully/slab system back toward the Taboo Glacier — the second station is on climber's left, the rest are straight down or climber's right. The crux of this option is the final rappel, where you must cross a moat/bergschrund to reach the snowfield below; this can be genuinely difficult and its condition can't be scoped from above, so the first person down should carry a picket, ice axe, and crampons to help climb out of the moat if needed. Bring two ropes (or a single rope doubled) for these double-rope rappels. (3) Continue over the summit and descend via the Torment-Forbidden Traverse toward Forbidden Peak (sustained exposure, a 5.6 step and ~45-degree snow/ice) if that's the day's objective — this is a full traverse, not a simple descent, and commits you to exiting via Forbidden's West Ridge/Boston Basin instead of returning the way you came.
hazards: Loose rock in the gullies, particularly pitches 3–4
Rockfall from parties above
Exposed traversing rappels on descent
Early-season snow/glacier crossing on approach

waysIn.name: Boston Basin, rising traverse to the Taboo Glacier
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount, directly opposite Johannesburg), take the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right turn onto the steep climbers' trail. Four small creek crossings, treeline about 5,300 ft, low camp 5,300-5,500 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp leave any semblance of trail and make a rising traverse to the northwest, holding roughly the 6,200 ft contour across talus, tundra and slab steps. You pass beneath the south spur of Forbidden Peak and cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above.

Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's-left side and follow it up. Some parties skip the summit-day traverse entirely by carrying up the Taboo and camping at about 7,100 ft directly beneath Torment's southeast face at the foot of the couloir.

This traverse is the part that gets people lost in cloud. It is open, uniform ground with no trail, and in early season the creek channels are buried and there is avalanche exposure across it.
hazards: Bergschrund or moat at the base of the couloir; a fatal accident on record
Loose Class 3-4 rock in the gully, with parties above and below
Featureless traverse from Boston Basin, easy to lose in whiteout
Early-season avalanche exposure on the traverse and buried creek channels
Couloir can be melted out to rock in late season
Short glacier crossing on the Taboo Glacier, firm snow or ice early season
Exposed traversing rappels on the descent

waysIn.name: Torment Basin climbers' path
waysIn.season: midsummer once brush is passable
waysIn.notes:
A separate and much less-used way in that skips Boston Basin altogether. Drive Cascade River Road only about 20 miles — roughly a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead — and look for the climbers' path starting about fifty feet upstream of the bridge over the Cascade River.

It is a steep, hard climb on a boot path that is mostly easy to follow up into Torment Basin, but despite decades of traffic some sections stay genuinely brushy. It puts you on the west side of the South Ridge rather than the east.

The reason to use it is the moat: from the Torment Basin side the South Ridge can be gained at about 6,600 ft without crossing the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier, which is the late-season crux of the standard approach. It is also the shorter drive.
hazards: Brushy sections on a steep unmaintained boot path
Less-travelled approach, so less current information on conditions
Loose crumbly rock on the climb and rockfall onto parties below
Exposed traversing rappels on the descent
Biting insects on the approach
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late season, when the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier makes the standard line hard; steeper and brushier on the approach.

name: Torment-Forbidden Traverse
approach: From the Boston Basin trailhead pullout on Cascade River Road (~3,300 ft, opposite Johannesburg Mountain, roughly mile 22-23), follow the old abandoned mining road for about 0.75 mile to the historic mine site. From there an unmaintained but well-beaten climbers' path takes over, switchbacking steeply up through forest with four creek/stream crossings to treeline around 5,300 ft. Above the trees the path eases across heather benches and talus into Boston Basin proper; low camp sits around 5,300-5,500 ft and high camp around 6,400 ft (total roughly 2.5-3 miles and 3,000-3,300 ft gain from car to high camp, 2.5-4 hours). A North Cascades NP backcountry permit (Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount) is required to camp. From high camp, leave the trail and make a rising, rightward (northwest) traverse across talus, tundra, and slab steps, crossing a couple of small creeks/snowmelt channels, staying beneath the cliff bands below Torment and Sahale, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above. Rope up at the glacier's toe and cross it heading for the notch that marks the base of Torment's climbing (on the standard line this is the same notch that starts the South Ridge). Watch for crevasses and a moat at the glacier's edge that can require careful stepping or a short awkward move to reach rock; a picket, axe, and crampons for the first person are worth carrying. Biting flies are notorious in Boston Basin in mid-summer, early-season snow can obscure the creek crossings and add avalanche exposure on the traverse, and whiteout conditions make the basin-to-glacier traverse genuinely easy to get lost in.
descent: The traverse finishes by descending Forbidden Peak, not Torment, so 'descent' here means the way off Forbidden's summit back to Boston Basin. From Forbidden's summit, downclimb and make about 3 rappels down the West Ridge (mostly in-situ slings on horns/blocks, some natural gear placements) back down to the West Ridge Notch below the false summit. From the notch, continue down the standard Forbidden couloir system known as the Cat Scratch Gullies - multiple parallel loose gullies separated by rock ribs; the accepted trick is to stay on the rib between gullies rather than descending gully bottoms, which funnel rockfall. Trip reports are inconsistent on exact rappel count here because it depends heavily on snow coverage and how much is downclimbed versus rappelled: parties report anywhere from about 5 to 10 rappels through this section (7 is the most commonly cited figure), generally on a mix of slung horns/chockstones and a few fixed anchors, with a 60m rope recommended (most individual raps are short enough for 30m but the last is longer). Do not skip anchors that look short - a couple of the short ones are there because the next station isn't visible. This funnels back down to the Forbidden-Torment glacier remnant and snowfields, from which you rejoin the Boston Basin traverse. All told, budget roughly 3 (West Ridge) + 5-7 (Cat Scratch) = about 8-10 rappels for the full descent. The waterfall-polished slabs just below the glacier at the bottom of this system have caught out descending parties (fatalities have occurred here) - downclimb them very carefully or locate the rappel anchors rather than improvising a scramble.
hazards: Rockfall, especially in the first half of the ridge and in the Cat Scratch Gullies on descent
Icefall off Torment's south face onto the approach/glacier
Crevasses and moats on the Taboo/Torment Glacier, worse late season
Long, sustained exposure on the knife-edge ridge with limited bail options once committed past Torment
Afternoon thunderstorms common in late summer

waysIn.name: Boston Basin high camp and the Taboo Glacier
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The traverse starts by climbing Torment's South Ridge, so the approach is the South Ridge approach. From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount), take the old mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. Four creek crossings, treeline at about 5,300 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft — call it 2.5-3 miles and 3,000-3,300 ft from the car.

From high camp traverse the upper basin northwest at roughly the 6,200 ft contour, beneath Forbidden's south spur, crossing a rock rib and a couple of snowmelt channels, heading for the toe of the Taboo Glacier and the lower South Ridge.

Because the traverse is long and committing, many parties instead carry over and camp at about 7,100 ft on the Taboo directly under Torment's southeast face at the foot of the east couloir, which turns a very long day into a reasonable one. Others bivy on the ridge partway across.

Overnight permits for Boston Basin are picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
hazards: Moat and bergschrund at the foot of the east couloir — fatal accident on record
Loose class 3-4 gully with parties above
Whiteout navigation across the basin-to-glacier traverse
Early-season avalanche exposure and buried creek crossings
Biting flies in Boston Basin in midsummer

name: Mount Townsend Trail (standard)
approach: Start at the Mt. Townsend Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,300 ft), reached via Forest Road 27 off Penny Creek Road out of Quilcene — the trailhead has a small gravel lot and a Buckhorn Wilderness boundary sign where Trail #839 begins. From the lot, the trail climbs immediately into dense, heavily wooded old-growth forest via the first of three switchback sets; this opening stretch is the steepest sustained grade on the route and stays shaded most of the way. After the initial switchbacks the trail eases through forest before a second switchback section, then a third set of steep, fully sun-exposed switchbacks that break out onto the crest of a ridge — this exposed stretch is the hottest, most water-demanding part of the hike in summer, so carry all the water you need (there is no reliable creek crossing directly on-trail; the small streams crossed in the first mile or so are often dry by late summer, so shallow Windy Lake by Camp Windy is the last water). At about 5,300 ft, roughly 2.6 miles in, an unmarked spur trail branches off to Windy Lake/Camp Windy, a common rest stop and the last reliable flat ground before the alpine section. Continuing on the main trail, at about 5,500 ft you reach the junction with the Silver Lakes Trail #842 — stay right (straight/uphill) to continue to the summit; the left fork toward Silver Lakes involves loose, unmaintained scrambling and is not the standard route. From this junction the forest opens into subalpine meadow and the trail's grade eases considerably for the final ~1 mile to the broad, flat summit ridge (6,282 ft), passing through increasingly open wildflower meadows with the last quarter-mile crossing mostly open, low-angle grassy/rocky tundra. No technical terrain or exposure is encountered on the standard route; the main hazards are heat/sun exposure on the third switchback set, lingering snow patches on the upper meadows into early summer (which can obscure the tread and create a slip hazard on a steep sidehill), and occasional route-finding uncertainty at the Silver Lakes junction if signage is missing.
descent: Descend via the same Trail #839 back to the Upper Trailhead — this is a straightforward out-and-back with no technical downclimbing, exposure, or rappelling anywhere on the route. From the summit meadows, retrace the trail down through the Silver Lakes Trail junction (stay right/downhill on #839), past the Windy Lake spur, and back down through the three switchback sections to the trailhead. The only descent-specific cautions are the same as on the way up: the exposed third (lowest) switchback set can be loose underfoot with pea gravel over hardpack, making for slippery footing especially with a full pack or in wet conditions, and lingering snow on the upper meadow section in early season can make the tread hard to follow on the descent if you're moving in fog or flat light — carrying a GPS track or map is prudent before mid-July in high-snow years. No rope or rappel gear is needed for this route at any point.
hazards: Lingering snow/ice on the upper trail and summit ridge into June in high-snow years - carry microspikes or an ice axe early season
Exposed, wind-scoured summit ridge with lightning risk during summer thunderstorms
Route-finding confusion at the Silver Lake Trail junction (3 mi) in fog or whiteout
Small Upper Trailhead lot (~12 cars) fills early on summer weekends, forcing roadside parking on narrow FR 27
Forest Road 27 is unmaintained in winter and can be gated or storm-damaged in shoulder seasons

waysIn.name: Mount Townsend Trail #839 from the Upper Trailhead
waysIn.season: Late June to October
waysIn.notes: Three sets of switchbacks, the last fully sun-exposed and the hottest, most water-hungry part of the day — there is no dependable creek on the trail itself. Camp Windy and an unmarked spur to Windy Lake sit at about 5,300 ft. The Lower Trailhead adds roughly two round-trip miles and five hundred feet. The small upper lot fills early on summer weekends.
hazards: Snow and ice on the upper trail and summit ridge into June in heavy years
Wind-scoured, lightning-exposed summit ridge in summer storms
Loose pea gravel over hardpack on the lowest switchback set
Steep open slope below the summit ridge holds consolidated snow
Route-finding confusion at the Silver Lakes junction in fog
No dependable creek on the trail; hot, exposed switchbacks
Small upper lot fills early on summer weekends

waysIn.name: Little Quilcene Trail over Little River Summit
waysIn.notes: The shortest way to the top, with the least gain. The trail climbs steadily through forest to Little River Summit, then follows an open, exposed ridge for the last mile to meet the main trail near the summit. Carry water, as the ridge is dry and sunny.
hazards: Open, exposed, dry ridge for the last mile, with no water
Wind-scoured, lightning-exposed summit ridge in summer storms
Snow and ice on the upper trail and summit ridge into June in heavy years
Route-finding confusion at the Silver Lakes junction in fog
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the small upper lot is full on a summer weekend, or for a quieter, mostly forested approach from the northeast; carry water for the dry exposed last mile.

name: Northeast Ridge
approach: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east to the Thornton Lakes Road spur (near milepost 117, just west of Newhalem) and follow the rough, unpaved, high-clearance road about 5 miles to the Thornton Lakes Trailhead (~2,500 ft). Hike the Thornton Lakes Trail — an old logging-road grade for the first ~2 miles, then steeper trail up to the ridge/pass (~4,900 ft) above the lakes — then descend to the lake outlet (~4,400-4,486 ft). Traverse the brushy, sometimes-faint climbers' path around the east/south side of middle Thornton Lake, then climb a long, loose scree/talus gully (roughly 1,200 ft of gain) to a col around 5,750-5,840 ft that serves as the standard bivy site.
descent: From the summit, downclimb roughly 30 ft off the north side of the notch to easier rock, then reverse the ridge via a long string of rappels (double-rope where two ropes are carried) interspersed with downclimbing — accounts report anywhere from about 7 to 10 rappels total, including a double-rope rappel off the crux crack pitch — back down to the bivy col. Existing slings and rap rings are present at most stations but the rock is loose, so back up or replace suspect anchors. From the col, reverse the approach gully and climbers' path back around Thornton Lake and out the Thornton Lakes Trail to the trailhead. On a late-September descent the third rappel used nearly all of a 60 m rope (a 57 m rope fell short), and some of the older anchors needed to be cut away and replaced; carry spare cord and full-length ropes.
hazards: Loose Skagit gneiss, especially on the upper ridge and final summit scramble.
Crevasse/moat hazard crossing the glacier remnant below the ridge, worse early season.
Long, complex multi-rappel descent on a loose, exposed ridge — errors here are a leading cause of epics on this route.

waysIn.name: Thornton Lakes Trail, the middle lake and the gully to the bivy col
waysIn.season: July through September, once the approach gully and the glacier remnant have melted out enough to reduce snow and icefall hazard. The gneiss on this ridge is considered unsafe wet or rimed, which keeps the route to a short dry-rock window.
waysIn.notes: From the highway near milepost 117, the Thornton Lakes spur road runs about five miles, rough and unpaved, to the trailhead; high clearance is worth having. The trail follows an old logging-road grade for the first couple of miles, then climbs more steeply to the ridge above the lakes before dropping to the lake outlet. Traverse the brushy, sometimes faint climbers' path around the east and south side of the middle lake, following the right bank of the stream, then make a high rising traverse and climb a long, loose scree and talus gully — on the order of twelve hundred feet of gain — northwest to a col at roughly 5,750 to 5,840 ft. That col is the standard bivy and the last place with reliable water; there is a second bivy two pitches up the ridge with room for about five people and no water at all, which saves time on the climbing day if you are willing to carry water to it. From the col, the ridge is gained by crossing the small pocket glacier remnant on the peak's eastern flank, which can be easy snow, or rock slabs and a bit of ice, depending on the season and the year.
hazards: rockfall and icefall from beneath the small receding glaciers on the north and east faces
loose gneiss, especially on the upper ridge and the final summit scramble
crevasse and moat hazard crossing the glacier remnant, worse early season
a long, complex multi-rappel descent on loose, exposed rock, which is where most epics on this route happen
old fixed slings and rings at most rappel stations on rock loose enough that anchors need backing up or replacing

name: The Needles Scramble
approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (~2,550 ft, end of FR 2870), start on the Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2, which runs a gentle, mostly level mile through old-growth forest along the Dungeness River to a well-signed junction. Bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail and settle into a steady, moderate climb up the Royal Creek valley for about 5 miles, crossing several tributary creeks — the last reliable water before the high basin — through forest that opens into wildflower meadows around the 6-mile mark, with Mount Clark and Mount Walkinshaw's 7,000-ft summits visible ahead. The trail steepens for the final push through switchbacks into Royal Basin, reaching Royal Lake (5,100 ft, ~7.2 mi, ~2,500 ft gain) — the established backcountry camp area (bear canisters required, no fires, permits needed May-Sept). From the lake, a climbers' path continues roughly another 0.8-1 mile and 500 ft of gain across willow flats and boulder benches to Upper Royal Basin (~5,600 ft, ~8 mi from the trailhead), the day-use staging area for all Needles-area objectives (camping is not permitted in the upper basin). Beyond Upper Royal Basin there is no maintained tread: traverse cross-country north, contouring below Mount Clark's east flank on talus and boulder benches toward Mount Walkinshaw, the northernmost peak in the Needles chain — this stretch is rough, adds roughly 1.5 miles and several hundred feet of ascending/descending sidehill travel, and involves genuine route-finding (krummholz and short cliff bands can obscure the best line, as noted by parties working this same traverse from the Gray Wolf Ridge side). Aim for the prominent talus tongue below Walkinshaw's broken east face, then climb northwest over boulders and a bare scree rib to the col at the south end of Gray Wolf Ridge, northeast of the peak. From the col, skirt several steepening pinnacles on their east side with Class 3 moves on rotten shale (far looser than typical Cascades granite), then follow the northeast ridge through ledges and small gullies to an exposed blade of rock and the small (~10-ft-diameter) rocky summit at 7,378 ft — Class 3 overall, with perhaps one short Class 4 step. Keep parties tight and helmets on through the entire gully/ridge section — loose rock and rockfall onto climbers below are the defining hazard of this route. Total round-trip distance from the trailhead is on the order of 19 miles (matching the route's recorded 30.58 km), reflecting the extra cross-country mileage beyond Upper Royal Basin that standard figures for the closer Royal Basin peaks (Deception/Mystery, ~14 mi RT) don't include.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the northeast ridge and pass the pinnacles back to the col, then descend the scree rib and talus to the base of the talus tongue, then retrace the cross-country traverse south below Mount Clark to Upper Royal Basin. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required on the standard northeast ridge line, and no fixed anchors or rappel stations are known to exist on it. The loose rock that makes the gully slow on the way up makes it just as slow (if not slower) coming down; downclimb facing in on the steeper sections, test holds before weighting them, and keep helmets on for the whole party the entire way down, since Olympic 'shale' rock is rotten and prone to breaking or sliding underfoot. Once back at Upper Royal Basin, follow the climbers' path back to Royal Lake and then the maintained Royal Basin Trail and Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 the full ~8 miles back to the trailhead. Given the length and elevation loss, budget real time and daylight for this descent — most parties treat the round trip as a long, full day (or a backpack with a camp at Royal Lake) rather than a quick out-and-back.
hazards: Loose, rotten Olympic sandstone/shale throughout the Needles — rockfall and holds that break underweight
Multiple similar gullies on the east face and northeast ridge make route-finding easy to botch in cloud or whiteout
Lingering snow/ice in the approach gullies into July in heavy-snow years
Long, remote approach with no cell coverage

waysIn.name: Upper Royal Basin and the north traverse under Clark
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Gentle forest mile to the signed fork, then a steady climb up the Royal Creek valley crossing tributaries — the last dependable water before the high basin. Steep switchbacks into Royal Basin, camp at the lake, then continue through the upper basin and cross-country north on talus and boulder benches beneath Clark's east flank, adding a rough mile and a half of sidehill.
hazards: Loose, rotten shale throughout the Needles, with holds that break under weight
Several parallel gullies on this flank that are easy to confuse in cloud
Rockfall onto anyone below in the gully — keep the party tight, helmets on
Snow and ice in the approach gullies into July in heavy-snow years
Krummholz and short cliff bands hiding the natural line on the traverse

name: Standard Scramble (above Lake Cushman)
approach: From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, continue right onto FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then turn left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage for roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead/parking area at about 3,026 ft. From here the 'trail' quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. The path climbs directly and steeply through forest for the first stretch, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, gaining several hundred feet before breaking out of the trees into a couple of open meadow benches (the most reliable early-season water, via lingering snowmelt seeps, is generally found in this meadow band — by mid-to-late summer expect it to be dry, so carry all the water you'll need from the car). Above the meadows the route enters scree and talus slopes and stays primarily on the climber's-left side of a large, loose rocky gully; this section is tight in spots with a lot of unconsolidated rock, so groups should stay spread out (not stacked directly above/below each other) to avoid raining rocks on people below. In spring and early summer this gully can hold avalanche-prone snow and may require an ice axe. The path winds above the gully until it gains Mount Washington's southern ridgeline, then follows a faint, exposed climbers'/goat trail along the ridge crest — in multiple spots the tread narrows to barely one boot-width with real exposure on both sides (this is the section referred to as the 'Dog Walk Ledge'); solid class 3 with a couple of class 3+/4 moves, and not a place for hesitant scramblers. The ridge trail leads to a scree field below the false summit (greasy and slick if wet) and a 'goat trail' up its climbers'-right edge to a stone wind shelter on the ridge, from which a final short class 3–4 scramble gains the true 6,255 ft summit.
descent: Descend the same ridge and gully line used on ascent — this is a walk-down/downclimb route with no fixed or standard rappels. From the summit, reverse the short class 3–4 step to the wind-shelter ridge, downclimb the scree field, and carefully re-trace the exposed 'Dog Walk Ledge' ridge-crest section facing in and moving one at a time through the narrowest, one-boot-width spots — this is the section most parties find harder and more nerve-wracking going down than coming up. Continue down the goat trail off the ridge into the gully and downclimb its climber's-left side back toward the meadows and treeline, again spreading the group out to avoid kicking loose rock onto anyone below. Some scramble parties carry a light rope, harness, and a rap device as a safety backup for this route — to lower packs, belay a nervous member through the exposed ridge crest, or rig a short rappel off a rock horn or tree if someone is uncomfortable downclimbing a specific class 4 move — but there are no bolted or fixed anchors anywhere on the route and a rope is not required for a competent scrambling party in dry conditions. Total descent retraces roughly 3,190 ft of loss back to the FR-2419 trailhead; parties commonly report the descent feeling slower than the climb up because of the steep, joint-jarring step-downs through the gully and forest.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the entry gullies and on the talus/scree slopes — stay tight as a group to avoid dislodging rock onto climbers below
Sustained exposure on the upper mountain, especially the 'catwalk' traverse and the exposed east-side/crest section near the summit
Steep, avalanche-prone snow in the gullies and on the saddle in spring/early season
Significant elevation loss on descent is hard on knees/ankles, especially late in a long day
Heat exposure — the route can be hot and muggy in summer with little shade above treeline
Route-finding difficulty through the forested lower section, meadows, and talus field, particularly in poor visibility

waysIn.name: FR-2419 up the Big Creek drainage to the road-end trailhead
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, best Jul-Sep. Spring and early summer put avalanche-capable snow in the gully
waysIn.notes:
From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, go right onto FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead at about 3,026 ft. Northwest Forest Pass to park; no wilderness permit is needed.

From here the trail quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. It climbs directly and steeply through forest, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, to a couple of open meadow benches around 3,800 ft. That meadow band holds the most reliable early-season water via snowmelt seeps; by mid-to-late summer expect it dry, so carry what you need from the car.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the entry gullies and on the talus — spread the group out rather than stacking above and below
Sustained exposure on the Dog Walk Ledge / Catwalk, where the tread is one boot wide with drops on both sides
Steep avalanche-prone snow in the gullies and on the saddle in spring and early season
The scree field below the false summit is greasy and slick when wet
Significant elevation loss on descent, hard on knees and ankles, and slower than the climb
Route-finding through the forested lower section, meadows and talus in poor visibility
Little shade above treeline; the route gets hot

waysIn.name: From Mount Ellinor, across the connecting ridge or the west-side basin
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes: Recorded as an approach because parties do reach Washington from Ellinor rather than from Big Creek, usually as half of a traverse. Ellinor is reached by Trail #812 from its Upper or Lower Trailhead, both on the same North Lake Cushman Road corridor, and from Ellinor's summit the connecting ridge runs northeast toward Washington. It is not a walk. The crest is fractured, weathered pillow basalt with sustained Class 4 scrambling past a series of gendarmes, and it carries a loose 50 ft downclimb that most parties call the least enjoyable part of the day. The alternative that several parties prefer is the west-side basin traverse: drop into the basin below the crest and cross it, rejoining Ellinor's standard winter route line rather than fighting the ridge. Used as an approach to Washington this is a long way round for a peak with a 3.2 km trail of its own, and it is here for traverse parties.
hazards: Fractured, weathered pillow basalt on the connecting ridge with a crux gendarme downclimb of notably poor rock and severe exposure
Sustained Class 4 scrambling past gendarmes with a loose 50 ft downclimb
Committing terrain between two summits with no quick exit
All the Washington summit-ridge hazards at the end of it
waysIn.whyThisWay: When traversing Mount Ellinor and Mount Washington in one day; a long way round if Washington is the only goal, with sustained Class 4 on the fractured ridge.

name: South/East Scramble
approach: Park at the Watson Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS Road 1107 (elev. ~4,300 ft), reached via Baker Lake Road (FS-11) south around Baker Lake on FS-1106 and out FS-1107 to road's end. From the trailhead, follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 into the woods; at about 1 mile you'll pass the junction with the Anderson Butte Trail #611.1 (stay straight/right for Watson Lakes). Around 1.5-2 miles, at roughly 4,700 ft, a second junction splits: right drops 0.5 mile to lower Anderson Lake, while the left fork climbs 0.5 mile to a small saddle entering the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness before dropping to the Watson Lakes (4,400 ft) near 2.5-3 miles in. The lakes are notoriously buggy in summer and are the last reliable water — treat before filling up, since there's no dependable source higher on the mountain. From Watson Lakes the maintained trail ends and the route becomes an open, cairned/boot-path climbers' route: leave the basin and climb talus (and snow well into summer) on Watson's north/west slopes toward the ridge crest. The standard and easiest line follows the widest gully east of the peak up to a saddle at about 5,900 ft on the ridge; a western gully alternative has a dangerous moat and rotten snow bridge late-season and should be avoided. From the 5,900-ft saddle, traverse along the ridge and across a steep slope to wrap around the base of the summit block. A short, loose class 2-3 dirt-and-rock gully (10-15 ft) gains the true summit ridge, which is a narrow (~30 ft), exposed class 2-3 catwalk with real drop-off on both sides — a hand line is commonly carried and recommended for this final airy section. Total round trip runs roughly 7-9.5 miles with 2,500-3,000 ft gain depending on exact trailhead/camp and route-finding; parties camping partway (e.g., ~5,400 ft on the north slopes) shorten the summit day considerably. Route-finding above the lakes is the main approach hazard in poor visibility since the line is unmarked talus/snow rather than trail.
descent: Descent reverses the ascent line in its entirety — this is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling (rappels: 0). From the summit, downclimb the exposed, narrow class 2-3 summit ridge (many parties use a hand line here) back down the short loose gully to the base of the summit block, then traverse back around the block and along the ridge to the 5,900-ft saddle. From the saddle, descend the east gully (the same talus/snow line used on the way up — avoid the west gully's moat/snow-bridge hazard) back into the basin above Watson Lakes, then pick up the maintained Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 at the lakes for the hike out to the trailhead, passing back through the two junctions (the ~4,700-ft Anderson/Watson Lakes fork, then the Anderson Butte Trail #611.1 junction at 1 mile from the trailhead). Descent times are typically close to ascent times (roughly 3+ hours from summit to car), consistent with a straightforward if loose reversal. Descent-specific hazards: loose talus and scree in the gully below the saddle, glissade/postholing risk on residual snow into midsummer, rotten moats/snow bridges if the west-side line is mistakenly used, and route-finding across the open, unmarked basin and ridge in flat light or fog — the exposed summit-ridge downclimb remains the technical crux in both directions.
hazards: Airy, exposed summit block/ridge (~30 ft) with drop-offs on both sides near the top
Moat and unstable snow bridge reported on the west-side approach gully — use the east gully instead
Lingering snow in the summit gully and on the saddle traverse into July, requiring an ice axe
Off-trail routefinding through talus and heather above the lakes
Heavy mosquito pressure at Anderson/Watson Lakes in summer

waysIn.name: Watson Lakes Trailhead, Trail #611 and the east gully to the saddle
waysIn.season: July through September is most reliable, though snow often lingers in the summit gully and on the saddle traverse into early July. Many parties prefer August for drier ground and fewer mosquitoes. An axe is worth carrying even in mid-summer.
waysIn.notes: Park at the end of the forest road above Baker Lake and follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail into the woods. At about a mile, stay right or straight where the Anderson Butte Trail climbs left toward the old lookout site. Around 4,700 ft a second junction splits: the right fork drops to lower Anderson Lake, the left fork climbs a short way to a small saddle at the wilderness boundary before dropping to the Watson Lakes. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and are the last reliable water, since nothing higher on the mountain runs dependably — treat before filling. The maintained trail ends there; from the basin the route becomes an open, cairned climbers' line up talus and, well into summer, snow. Established bivy sites on open slopes around 5,400 ft shorten the summit day considerably. Route-finding across the unmarked basin and ridge in flat light is the main difficulty of the approach, since there is no tread to follow.
hazards: a moat and unstable snow bridge that develop in the west-side gully late season
lingering snow in the summit gully and on the saddle traverse into July
an airy summit ridge with drop-offs on both sides near the top
off-trail route-finding through talus and heather above the lakes, with nothing marked
loose talus and scree in the gully below the saddle on the descent
heavy mosquito pressure at the lakes through summer

name: Mount Wilder Scramble
approach: Mount Wilder sits deep in the Elwha drainage and this is a genuine multi-day backpack approach, not a day hike-in. From the Whiskey Bend trailhead (reached by an extra ~7-mile road-walk/bike-in from Madison Falls, where Olympic Hot Springs Road has been closed to vehicles since November 2017 flood damage), follow the Elwha River Trail south along the river's east bank through old-growth lowland forest. Established waypoints/camps along the way (mileages approximate, gathered from NPS and trip-report cross-referencing): the Humes Ranch cutoff around 2.7 mi, Lillian River Camp around 4.9 mi (reliable water, log crossing of the Lillian River), Mary's Falls around 8.8 mi, Canyon Camp around 9.6 mi (trail narrows through a rocky gorge section), Elkhorn around 11.4 mi (old guard-station clearing, bear wire), and Hayes River Guard Station around 16 mi (junction with the Hayes River/Dodger Point trail). Continue upriver to Camp Wilder, roughly 20 miles from Whiskey Bend (established campsites, bear wire, small shelter), which sits in the river bottom east of the peak and is the logical base camp for the climb. Water is abundant along the river trail (numerous tributary crossings) but there is no bridge maintenance guarantee on side creeks — expect to rock-hop or ford minor tributaries, higher and faster in early season. From Camp Wilder there is no maintained trail to the summit: leave the river trail and climb off-trail, first through streamside brush and old forest, then heather benches and talus, to gain the peak's south ridge. The south aspect of Mount Wilder rises nearly 3,800 feet in under two miles, so expect sustained, steep, trail-less travel on a mix of open slope, talus, and brush, with real route-finding needed to link the cleanest line to the ridge crest — there is no cairned or established scramble path, and this peak has no recorded first ascent date, reflecting how rarely it's visited. Top off water at Camp Wilder or a tributary before starting the climb, since it is scarce higher on the ridge.
descent: Descend via the same south ridge/slope line used on the ascent — this is a class 2 walk-off scramble with no technical downclimbing and no rappelling required. The main hazards are route-finding (it is easy to drift off the true ridge crest onto steeper, brushier terrain or loose rock bands in the talus/heather zone, especially in poor visibility) and loose rock and scree on the steep upper slopes underfoot. Take careful mental notes of ascent landmarks — drainages, rock outcrops, benches — since the featureless heather/talus terrain looks different in descent light and it's easy to cliff out above the steep lower slopes if you wander from the ascent line. The terrain naturally funnels back toward the river valley, so keep trending toward the Elwha drainage to return to Camp Wilder. From Camp Wilder, retrace the Elwha River Trail roughly 20 miles back to Whiskey Bend (plus the current road-walk/bike-in if the Whiskey Bend Road washout is still in effect).
hazards: Long, remote off-trail approach with genuine route-finding difficulty through brush and timber
Elwha River ford hazard, notably near Chicago Camp — can run high and dangerous; check current conditions before relying on it
Lingering snow on upper slopes into July
The 'Elwha Snowfinger,' once a common approach/exit shortcut into the upper Elwha Basin, has receded and is no longer considered reliably passable
No cell coverage — multi-day self-rescue timeframe if injured
Black bears present in the Elwha corridor — proper food storage required

name: Standard Route / South Side
approach: From the large pullout on the inside of the Hairpin Turn on SR-20 (~Milepost 163, roughly 5,150 ft, just below Washington Pass), drop off the highway shoulder and ford Early Winters Creek directly across from the parking area — expect wet feet in early-season high water; by mid-to-late summer it braids down to an easy rock-hop. From the far bank, head straight up into timber on climber's-left of the obvious drainage gully that falls from Kangaroo Ridge; a boot-path stays in the trees rather than fighting brush in the gully bottom itself. As the trees thin, keep to the left side of the gully and follow it onto the ridge crest above, mixing dirt/heather benches with short bouts of easy Class 2-3 scrambling. This is the shared approach line for all of the Kangaroo Ridge towers (Big Kangaroo, Half Moon, Mushroom Tower) and packs about 3,000 ft of gain into well under 2 miles, so it is steep and sustained the whole way — plan on 2.5-4 hours up for a party unfamiliar with it. Where the ridge steepens below the final rock tiers, traverse left beneath the base of the wall and climb a band of steep snow (a snowfinger that lingers on this shaded aspect well into summer) to reach the notch/base directly under Mushroom Tower's summit block; an ice axe is standard here and crampons are worth carrying in early season, when this stretch can hold enough snow to kick steps the whole way. There is no reliable water above the initial creek ford, so treat that crossing as your last easy fill-up. There is no maintained trail or trail number above the highway — it is entirely a climber's boot-path, and route-finding is straightforward in clear weather (aim for the mushroom-capped tower on the skyline) but unforgiving in fog or whiteout given the mix of gully, timber, and traverse terrain.
descent: The route tops out with a short, exposed step/traverse across a gap just below the true summit block, which is the technical crux and can be wet or verglassed when snow is still sitting on top of the tower. Descent from the summit is a single rappel — well under one rope length — off a fixed anchor of two old 1/4-inch bolts placed by Fred Beckey's party during the June 1942 first ascent of the Kangaroo Ridge towers. Treat it as decades-old hardware: inspect it closely before trusting it and back it up (or extend/replace) if you're carrying the means to do so. A standard doubled rope (e.g., a 60m rope folded to give 30m per strand, or even a doubled 30m rope) reaches with room to spare; a single-strand rappel on a 30m+ rope would also work if that suits your retrieval plan. The rappel lands on south-side scramble terrain; from there, downclimb/scramble back to the notch and reverse the ascent traverse and snowfinger to the head of the approach gully. Descend the same climber's-left line used on the way up — the gully commonly holds snow late into the season and can be partially glissaded, which speeds the descent but carries runout and rockfall-channel exposure once the snow softens in the afternoon sun, so timing matters. Continue down through timber to Early Winters Creek, re-ford, and you're back at the Hairpin Turn pullout. This is not a walk-off: even though the technical climbing is short (2 pitches), the exposed summit step and the fixed-anchor rappel mean a rope, harness, and rappel device are mandatory gear, not optional. Round-trip car-to-car time for a party familiar with the route runs roughly 6-8 hours.
hazards: Loose, eroded, granular granite low on the approach (better rock higher up)
Talus/scree approach that becomes ankle-twisting 'leg breakers' once snow cover melts off
Steep snow in the approach gully, especially before mid-July
Aged 1/4-inch bolt rappel anchor of undocumented current condition

name: Mutchler Peak Scramble
approach: Park at the Cascade River Road washout roughly 14.2 miles from Marblemount, about 100 yards past the Cascade River crossing near the FR 1570 junction (signed for Kindy Ridge/Found Lake). The old FR 1570 spur is now permanently closed to vehicles, so the hike starts on the abandoned roadbed near Vee Creek at roughly 1,150-1,400 ft — parties note the washed-out culvert and downed timber (one log up to 4 ft across) blocking the road about 0.8 mile in. Follow the old road/boot path, crossing several windfalls, to an old firepit near a reliable creek (last easy water before the ridge). From the firepit the unmaintained climbers' path turns steep immediately, threading old-growth forest on exposed roots with occasional spur tracks around blowdown; expect the tread to fade into debris in places — this stretch to the Found Peak area (roughly 2.5 miles, gaining ~2,500-3,000 ft) is the main route-finding crux of the approach. The path dips to a broad saddle near 4,800 ft where the boot path is easy to lose; parties often end up scrambling 300-400 ft above the pass before relocating the trail, then follow it up through grass and boulders (~600 ft) into a meadow with Found Lake below (pools here are not reliably potable). From there the route climbs over Point 5695 and drops to a second saddle before joining Kindy Ridge proper: a broad, mostly open granite ridge combining faint tread and easy slab-hopping, steep but non-technical, with constant views toward Snowking Mountain, Mutchler Peak, and the Cyclone Lake basin. Camps are commonly made near 6,200 ft on the ridge or down at Cyclone Lake (a strikingly turquoise tarn-fed lake); a small stream south of the ridge camp and a tarn just above Cyclone Lake are the best water sources up high. From the ridge/Cyclone Lake basin, Mutchler Peak's summit block is reached by heather and blocky rock slopes rising out of the basin — moderate Class 2-3 scrambling with some loose rock near the top; no published figure gives the car-to-summit distance for Mutchler itself, but Snowking, reached by the same approach over Kindy Ridge, is roughly 16-18 miles round trip. Because the approach is entirely unmaintained (no official trail, no numbered Forest Service trail), competent off-trail navigation is required, and this is a long, full-day-plus approach — most parties treat it as an overnight rather than a single push.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down Mutchler's heather and blocky rock flanks into the Cyclone Lake basin, then back up and over the Found Peak/Kindy Ridge saddle system to the 4,800 ft saddle and down through the old-growth/windfall section to the firepit and abandoned FR 1570 roadbed, then out to the Cascade River Road washout. This is a walk-off/downclimb the entire way — no rappelling is involved on the scramble route or its descent. The main descent hazards are route-finding (the boot path through the meadow/saddle area above Found Peak is easy to lose in both directions and there are cliff bands nearby to avoid), loose rock and heather on the steep upper slopes off Mutchler's summit, and fatigue-driven navigation errors on the long unmaintained stretch back to the road, especially if daylight runs short — at least one trip report specifically mentions avoiding a creek-bed shortcut on the way out after dark in favor of staying on the known road/trail line.
hazards: Loose, blocky rock typical of North Cascades scrambling terrain
Steep heather and slab that become slick and hazardous when wet or dewy
Lingering snow and ice on north-facing gullies and slopes into July
Difficult route-finding through cliff bands below Point 5791 on the Kindy Ridge approach
Dense brush, slide alder, and devil's club on the lower approach where the old road bed is overgrown
Swollen creek crossings (Cascade River, Kindy/Mutchler Creek) during peak snowmelt
Crevasses and glide cracks on the Mutchler Glacier
A cornice on the ridge above Cyclone Lake in early summer

name: Narcos
approach: This is a distinct approach from the one used for Cutthroat Peak, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass with no maintained trail. For Cutthroat Wall, start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail #483 from the Cutthroat Trailhead kiosk. After a short distance on the main trail, leave it via a cairned path that cuts into the forest, then follow cairns and a climbers' path (roughly 1.5-2 miles, 45 min-2 hrs total) through brush and talus, trending toward the buttress, to reach the base of Cutthroat Wall.
descent: Because P4-P5 merge into Wright-Pond's corner and final pitch, the standard descent is to rappel down the Wright-Pond line: 4 double-rope (60m) raps back to the base.
hazards: Vegetated/dirty cracks, especially in less-traveled lower pitches
Runout PG13 terrain on P3-P4
Loose rock possible given the route's limited traffic
