waysIn.name: Cutthroat Creek Trailhead and the forest traverse to the wall's right side
waysIn.season: Late June through September, matching the neighbouring crags on the same approach. Early-season parties should expect bushier, dirtier cracks, since this wall sees very little traffic and the cracks have not been cleaned by use.
waysIn.notes: Turn off the highway a little over four miles east of Washington Pass, following signs for the Cutthroat Creek trail, and drive about a mile to the trailhead lot, which has restrooms. Do not confuse this with the Cutthroat Peak approach, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout well west of here and serves a different objective entirely. Start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail, then leave it a short way along and walk up through the woods toward the wall — the ground gains elevation quickly at first, then the line traverses leftward through open forest and across slabby benches. There is no maintained tread on this section; parties report cairns and an intermittent climbers' path, but treat it as open-forest navigation rather than a trail. The traverse ends on a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side, which is where the climbing starts. Allow the better part of a couple of hours from the car to the base.
hazards: vegetated and dirty cracks, especially on the less-travelled lower pitches
runout terrain on the middle pitches
loose rock, given how rarely the wall is climbed
open-forest and slab navigation with no maintained trail to the base

name: South Slopes
approach: Start at the Stafford Creek Trailhead (Trail #1359), Cle Elum Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, at the end of Stafford Creek Road (FR 9703), which leaves North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) past 29 Pines Campground — a small, often-overflowing lot for roughly 20 cars (Northwest Forest Pass required). From the trailhead, Stafford Creek Trail #1359 climbs at a gentle-to-moderate grade through dry ponderosa/lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek for the first mile (a short rerouted, steeper switchback section around 0.5 mile bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread). The trail continues gaining gradually along the creek — figure roughly 3,000 ft of gain spread over the approach — reaching a signed junction with the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) at about 3.5–3.8 miles; this crossing of Stafford Creek is the last reliable, easy water source before the high country and is worth topping off here. Bear right (east/north) at the junction to stay on the Navaho Pass approach. Around 4.5 miles the trail opens into a large, marshy subalpine meadow with established campsites and a feeder stream — the usual base camp for parties splitting the trip over two days, and another water source. Beyond camp the trail crosses the barren, eroded 'Moon Landing' stretch (sparse vegetation, serpentine/greenstone talus) before a final push to Navaho Pass (~6,000 ft) around mile 5.5. A commonly used shortcut leaves the main trail where two creek forks merge around the 3-mile mark, climbing steep, loose slopes directly up the northeast-facing drainage to the col below Navaho's southeast ridge — it saves close to 2 miles of trail hiking but is steeper, unmaintained, and involves loose scree/dirt, so most parties use it only for one direction of the trip. Total car-to-summit is on the order of 11–13 miles round trip with about 4,000–4,200 ft of gain depending on which junction/shortcut combination is used. Note: several miles of this trail burned in the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire. Its closure order has been lifted and the trail is open, as the Cle Elum Ranger District's trail crew reported on September 25, 2026, but expect burned forest and dead trees along the corridor. A second off-trail variant leaves the trail right after the Stafford Creek crossing and climbs directly into the open bowl between Earl Peak and Navaho Peak to about 5,000 ft, scrambles north to the ridgeline near 6,000 ft, then follows the west/southwest ridge to the summit — a different line than the northeast-drainage shortcut.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: drop off the summit back down the broad south/southeast ridge to Navaho Pass (easy Class 2 scrambling, no rope or rappelling needed), then rejoin Stafford Creek Trail #1359 and retrace it past the Moon Landing section, the meadow camp/water source, the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) junction at ~3.5–3.8 miles, and back down along Stafford Creek to the trailhead. Parties who used the creek-fork shortcut on the way up sometimes descend the standard pass-and-trail route instead (or vice versa) to make a rough loop, but both options are plain hiking/scrambling terrain — there is no rappelling on this route. Watch for loose scree and dirt on the steeper shortcut drainage if descending that way, and expect possible lingering snow near the pass and on the upper ridge into early-mid summer, which can make the descent line slicker than the ascent.
hazards: Lingering snowfields on the upper bowl/ridge into July — can obscure the route and create fall/glissade hazard on steep sections
Afternoon thunderstorms with lightning exposure on the open ridge and summit
Loose talus and blocky terrain above ~6,000 ft — rockfall risk onto parties below
Burned forest from the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire along Trail #1359: hazard trees and fire-damaged tread
Long, mostly waterless upper approach — carry sufficient water

waysIn.name: Stafford Creek Trail #1359 to Navaho Pass
waysIn.season: July into October. Snow patches linger on the upper ridge into July, when poles and light traction are worthwhile.
waysIn.notes: From the small road-end lot, Trail #1359 leaves at an easy grade through dry ponderosa and lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek; a short rerouted section of steeper switchbacks near the half-mile mark bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread. The creek crossing in the meadows is the last easy water and worth topping off at. Stay on #1359 at the signed Standup Creek Trail junction, and the trail opens into a large marshy subalpine meadow with a feeder stream and established campsites — the usual overnight base. Above the meadow the tread leaves the trees and switchbacks up open, rocky, sparsely vegetated slope for the last stretch to the pass.
hazards: No water and essentially no shade above the meadows, on ground that bakes on a warm afternoon
Loose scree over dirt on the climbers' path onto the ridge, steepening quickly and easy to push down onto a party below
Lingering snow patches into July
Slopes on either flank of the summit ridge are looser and steeper than they look from above
Several miles of the trail run through the 2025 burn: dead and burned trees can fall, especially in wind

name: North Ridge
approach: Needle Peak is only reachable by boat or floatplane: ride the Lady of the Lake ferry (or a Chelan Airways floatplane) up 50-mile-long Lake Chelan from the town of Chelan to Stehekin Landing — there is no road access from the outside world. From Stehekin Landing, take the Stehekin Valley Road (or the NPS shuttle) about 11 miles up-valley to High Bridge, where the road crosses the Stehekin River and the Pacific Crest Trail comes down off Cottonwood Camp and continues south as the Agnes Creek Trail. Follow the PCT/Agnes Creek Trail (National Park Service-maintained, gentle grade through old-growth forest along Agnes Creek) roughly 8-9 miles south to Swamp Creek Camp (about 2,800 ft), a designated PCT camp and the standard base for the peak — most parties treat this as an overnight approach rather than a single push. From camp, leave the PCT and pick up the unmaintained Swamp Creek Trail heading north/northeast up the Swamp Creek drainage; expect heavy blowdown, erosion, and brush-choked tread that has seen little maintenance in years. Cross Swamp Creek itself on a large fallen log around 3,600 ft (a small waterfall near 3,500 ft and a side stream joining Swamp Creek near 5,200 ft are the last reliable water before the upper mountain, though both can thin out late season). Around 3,200 ft, below Needle's north/south ridge system, most parties leave the Swamp Creek Trail proper and climb a steep, brushy slope directly toward the peak, working through dense foliage and sloping slabs. Near 5,000 ft a polished, slick slab gully is best avoided by staying west through a band of rocks; above that the line continues over talus and (even in summer) lingering snow, aiming for the prominent 7,300 ft notch on Needle's north side, below the steep north ridge and face rising above Swamp Creek, that gives the route its character. Watch for wobbly, loose-grained blocks on the upper talus and near the notch, wasp nests in the brush lower down, and route-finding difficulty in the unmaintained brush sections — this is a full mountaineering day (or two) from camp, not a casual scramble.
descent: Descend the same north-ridge line used on ascent: from the summit, reverse the class 3 gully above the notch (some parties find an alternate exposed gully slightly east of the ascent line that looks manageable from above but funnels into the same terrain) and downclimb to the crux 7,300-7,400 ft notch. This notch is the one place on the route where parties differ — many downclimb it unroped on adequate but exposed hand/footholds, while others back off with a single rappel of roughly 30 m/100 ft. There is no fixed or bolted rappel station here: any anchor is a natural one (slung block, horn, or krummholz/tree) built by the descending party, and old rappel webbing/cord has been reported at the notch by multiple parties of unclear age and origin — treat any found tat as unverified and back it up or replace it rather than trusting it outright. Below the notch, work back down through the talus and snow, staying on the west side of the cliff bands to avoid the steeper, more exposed rock, then pick back through the polished slab gully near 5,000 ft (stemming with the help of trees rooted in the cracks helps on the slicker sections) and down the brushy slope to rejoin the unmaintained Swamp Creek Trail around 3,200 ft. Follow Swamp Creek Trail back down to Swamp Creek Camp on the PCT (re-crossing Swamp Creek on the same log around 3,600 ft), then retrace the Agnes Creek Trail/PCT roughly 8-9 miles to High Bridge and the Stehekin Valley Road for the shuttle or walk back to Stehekin Landing and the ferry. No technical descent gear beyond a single rope/rack for the optional notch rappel is needed; the rest is a sustained, loose, brushy class 2-3 walk-down with real route-finding demands.
hazards: Loose, 'wobbly' rock and an eroded, polished slab low on the route
Significant exposure at the north-ridge crux (7,300-7,400 ft) with an airy notch downclimb
Old, unvetted rappel webbing left in place at the crux by previous parties — inspect or back it up before trusting it
Wasp nests reported in the approach brush and lower slopes, especially late summer
Fully unmaintained route beyond Swamp Creek Camp — bushwhacking, deadfall, and route-finding required
No cell coverage; remote, rarely-visited peak with long evacuation times

waysIn.name: Agnes Creek crest trail to Swamp Creek Camp and the ridge
waysIn.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends. Snow lingers on the upper talus even in summer.
waysIn.notes: No road reaches this valley: take the passenger ferry or a floatplane up the lake to the landing, then the valley road or the shuttle up to the bridge at the road end, and plan the whole trip around those timetables. Walk a few hundred yards up the road to pick up the crest trail heading south, then follow well-graded tread through old-growth forest into the Agnes Creek valley past the first creekside camp, and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork — the standard overnight base. The peak shows itself up-valley along that stretch. From camp pick up the unmaintained trail up the Swamp Creek drainage, with blowdown, eroded tread, heavy brush and a crossing of Swamp Creek on a large downed log, and leave it near 3,200 ft below the ridge.
hazards: The Swamp Creek path is unmaintained and heavily overgrown, with wasps a recurring nuisance in the brush
About 1,800 ft of trackless steep brushy climbing on vegetation, dirt and small rock steps
A slick polished slab at the head of the gully near 5,000 ft, bypassed with a rope and a tree belay
Serious exposure above the talus field and loose, wobbly blocks near the notch and on the summit ridge
No water on the ridge — it has to be carried up from below
The crest overhangs near the top and the last stretch drops into a narrow gully that has to be reversed or rappelled
